articles.title: Supporting creative agency: metacognitive control and trust in generative AI art education
articles.author: Renhao Zhu
articles.summary: This paper employs a quantitative multimethod design to extend the UTAUT framework for generative AI (GenAI) adoption among art students. Study 1 tested the integrated model via structural equation modeling using cross-sectional survey data from 450 Chinese art students and developed a trust construct grounded in instrumental technology trust, supplemented by art-value-aligned items. Trust in GenAI showed the strongest direct association with behavioral intention (β = 0.425). Social influence was the dominant correlate of trust (β = 0.262), with 42.1% of its total effect mediated indirectly through trust. Metacognitive control showed a positive direct association with behavioral intention (β = 0.146), alongside an indirect association through trust. The structural model based on survey data explained 59.7% of the variance in behavioral intention. Study 2 used a between-subjects experiment with 80 art students to test whether situational metacognitive prompting causally affected creative output. Participants receiving metacognitive prompts (Group A) obtained higher expert ratings than the control group (Group B) on semantic content (d = 0.67), visual style (d = 1.30), and spatial composition (d = 0.63); within-group feature-distance analyses also indicated greater output diversity in Group A across all three dimensions. These findings suggest that trust and metacognitive control are key pathways in GenAI adoption for artistic creation, and that low-cost situational metacognitive prompting may enhance both the quality and diversity of AI-assisted artworks.

articles.bodyText:
This paper employs a quantitative multimethod design to extend the UTAUT framework for generative AI (GenAI) adoption among art students. Study 1 tested the integrated model via structural equation modeling using cross-sectional survey data from 450 Chinese art students and developed a trust construct grounded in instrumental technology trust, supplemented by art-value-aligned items. Trust in GenAI showed the strongest direct association with behavioral intention (β = 0.425). Social influence was the dominant correlate of trust (β = 0.262), with 42.1% of its total effect mediated indirectly through trust. Metacognitive control showed a positive direct association with behavioral intention (β = 0.146), alongside an indirect association through trust. The structural model based on survey data explained 59.7% of the variance in behavioral intention. Study 2 used a between-subjects experiment with 80 art students to test whether situational metacognitive prompting causally affected creative output. Participants receiving metacognitive prompts (Group A) obtained higher expert ratings than the control group (Group B) on semantic content (d = 0.67), visual style (d = 1.30), and spatial composition (d = 0.63); within-group feature-distance analyses also indicated greater output diversity in Group A across all three dimensions. These findings suggest that trust and metacognitive control are key pathways in GenAI adoption for artistic creation, and that low-cost situational metacognitive prompting may enhance both the quality and diversity of AI-assisted artworks.

Introduction

Technological innovation drives educational reform. Generative AI (GenAI), which processes unstructured textual and visual data, has reshaped learning and knowledge production (Murugesan and Cherukuri, 2023). Consequently, scholars and practicing educators have begun to examine how GenAI tools reshape the logic of human learning, modes of knowledge production, and future career structures (Dwivedi et al., 2023). Although GenAI offers substantial educational benefits, the academic community should move beyond merely worrying about risks to teaching standards and instead explore reasonable, standardized guidelines for its use by students and scholars (Susarla et al., 2023). However, the adoption of emerging technologies is a gradual psychological process that poses a significant challenge for art students in higher education. Artistic creation itself relies on the personal styles and values that creators have developed over time. Students are generally concerned that integrating GenAI into the creative process may undermine their artistic autonomy. This concern has further slowed the adoption of GenAI. This paper adopts two complementary studies with distinct research aims. Study 1 used cross-sectional survey-based structural equation modeling to test the psychological adoption pathway: metacognitive control shapes art students’ behavioral intention to use GenAI both directly and indirectly via trust in GenAI. Study 2 employed complementary triangulation a between-subjects laboratory experiment to manipulate situational metacognitive prompts and examine their causal links to aesthetic quality and output diversity of AI-assisted artworks. The two studies adopt complementary triangulation. Study 2 does not test the trust-mediation pathway established in Study 1, as it focuses on creative-output outcomes instead of behavioral intention.

Literature review

Most research on AI adoption in education still operates within the technology acceptance tradition. Studies in art and design education have largely extended these technology acceptance frameworks to identify the antecedents of students’ intention to use AI tools. This body of work has considerable value, but it rests on assumptions that are in tension with the actual process of artistic creation.

The first problem is conceptual: how “trust” is defined. In mainstream educational technology research, trust is treated as confidence in system stability and data security (Tarhini et al., 2017a). In artistic settings, students’ trust in AI is inseparable from normative judgments about authorship, the authenticity of the work, and aesthetic autonomy (Grassini and Koivisto, 2025). Acceptance models built on utilitarian beliefs have no vocabulary for this value-laden dimension, and so they tend to miss the very concerns that shape art students’ decisions.

The second is theoretical. Metacognitive control has largely been left out of the story: the literature has not explained how learners plan, monitor, and coordinate with AI during human–machine collaboration (Bian et al., 2025; Xu, 2025). The omission matters, because metacognitive control is central to creative ideation: task focus, goal-oriented strategy use, and effective creative screening each independently predict divergent creativity (Benedek and Lebuda, 2025). Without this pathway, acceptance models offer no account of how students actively regulate their cognitive processes while working with generative systems.

The third is empirical. Existing studies mostly verify main effects; they rarely trace how external technological conditions are converted into internal motivation through psychological mediating variables (Sáez-Velasco et al., 2024; Marqués Ibáñez and Delgado Hernández, 2025). GenAI can enhance mental flexibility and novelty by supplying divergent stimulus material (Tigre Moura et al., 2023), yet critics argue that reliance on algorithm-generated content fosters cognitive homogenization and weakens creative agency (Pan et al., 2025). The likely hinge between these outcomes is the user’s degree of control: minimal, directive prompts combined with passive acceptance tend to yield formulaic outputs, whereas active control and iterative refinement allow AI to amplify creativity (Sherson et al., 2023). Artistic creation, being open-ended and affectively charged, is precisely where this hinge matters most; because AI lacks intentionality and aesthetic sensibility, the human’s analytic and interpretive role remains irreplaceable (Wingström et al., 2024). Therefore, this study aims to extend the UTAUT-based technology acceptance model by examining whether art students’ GenAI use correlates with these new constructs, and by experimentally testing the causal effects of situational metacognitive prompting on the aesthetic quality and output diversity of AI-assisted artworks.

Theoretical framework and research hypotheses

Theoretical distinctiveness of GenAI-supported artistic creation

The Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) is a widely used framework for studying information-technology user adoption. It helps researchers explain how users form attitudes toward and trust in GenAI and other emerging technologies (Venkatesh et al., 2003). Traditional UTAUT models aim to explain the adoption of information technology that functions primarily as a tool-based system. These constructs assume that adoption is largely a matter of functional evaluation and social conformity. For bounded, efficiency-oriented tasks, these assumptions are reasonable. However, for GenAI-supported artistic creation, art-generation processes have moved beyond simple linear task execution toward interactive, dialogue-like collaborative work. Beyond its core tool-related attributes of stability and reliability, GenAI also carries context-specific artistic considerations: originality, safety, and algorithmic fairness. In this context, the core issue of adoption is not merely whether GenAI is useful or easy to use, but whether it can be trusted as a legitimate medium for artistic creation.

GenAI-driven artistic creation is open-ended rather than bounded. This stems not only from its interactive nature during task work but also from differences between artistic and industrial evaluation standards. Artistic creation has no clear stopping criteria and thus demands ongoing monitoring, strategic adjustment, and iterative optimization. Metacognitive control has been theorized as an internal agency mechanism distinct from facilitating conditions. It directly influences behavioral intentions by providing strategic capabilities and a sense of authorial control, and indirectly influences behavioral intentions by reducing “black-box anxiety” and enhancing trust.

This study makes three modifications to the original UTAUT. First, use behavior was removed. The primary reason was that the survey’s inclusion criteria restricted the sample to art students who had already used GenAI in their disciplinary studies. As a result, “whether to use” was largely predetermined, and a use-behavior measure would suffer from restricted variance, selection bias, and ceiling effects, substantially weakening its appropriateness and explanatory power. A secondary reason is that self-reported Use behavior in cross-sectional data is vulnerable to common method bias, social desirability, and reverse causality; moreover, GenAI use is highly heterogeneous, ranging from casual exploration to iterative creation, making it difficult to quantify uniformly by frequency or time. Therefore, Study 2 provided complementary behavioral evidence by experimentally examining creative output diversity.

Second, facilitating conditions were modeled as antecedents of behavioral intention rather than of use behavior. Because this study does not adopt use behavior as the dependent variable, the original UTAUT path from FC to use behavior was no longer applicable. Subsequent extensions suggest that in early-stage educational technology adoption, external resources and support are better understood as enabling conditions that shape users’ willingness to adopt. In GenAI-supported artistic creation, the availability of hardware, training, and assistance does not automatically produce creative use; it first increases perceived manageability of the creative process and reduces uncertainty and risk, thereby strengthening trust in GenAI and directly enhancing behavioral intention. We therefore model FC → BI (H3) and FC → Trust (H7) to capture how external conditions were converted into behavioral intention and value-laden trust, rather than directly producing use behavior.

Third, regarding the newly added GenAI trust construct, this study acknowledges that it partially overlaps with traditional technology trust. However, this overlap was not a theoretical flaw; rather, it represents a reasonable extension and contextualization. The scale was adapted from an established technology trust scale to the artistic context and refined in a pilot study. This pilot study (N = 121) was conducted prior to the main survey, using the same recruitment method as the main survey: participants were art majors who met the same inclusion criteria, and the study was distributed through the network of teachers in Zhejiang. It is important to note that the pilot study sample was independent of the 450 participants in Study 1 and is not included in that study. During the pilot, the trust scale initially included two authorship-related items (BHA1 and BHA3) in addition to the five retained trust items (TI1–TI5). An exploratory factor analysis (EFA) with principal axis factoring and varimax rotation revealed a clear two-factor structure: the five trust items loaded on the first factor (loadings 0.714–0.788), whereas the two authorship items loaded cleanly on a separate second factor (BHA3 = 0.845; BHA1 = 0.773) with no cross-loadings on the trust factor (Supplementary Table S3). Because these two items formed a distinct factor that was not theoretically consistent with a unidimensional trust construct, they were removed at the EFA stage to preserve a single-factor trust scale for the CFA.

Within the final five-item scale, TI1 (functional reliability), TI3 (safety and privacy), and TI5 (overall reliability) overlapped with traditional technology trust, and this overlap constituted the foundational core of trust: students must first believe that the system can operate stably and protect their works and data. However, foundational trust alone is insufficient to explain adoption decisions in the artistic context, because students also care about whether generated content is original, whether authorship is respected, and whether the algorithm is fair. Therefore, TI2 (originality and authorship) and TI4 (algorithmic fairness) reflected the value-laden dimensions specific to artistic creation. Because only two of the five retained items capture art-specific concerns, we described the construct as primarily instrumental trust with an art-value supplement.

Variables under the unified theory of acceptance and use of technology (UTAUT)

This study draws on theoretical extensions in subsequent research on technology acceptance to treat facilitating conditions as direct antecedents influencing behavioral intention. Chen et al. (2026) investigated older adult learners’ acceptance of generative AI and reported a substantial, statistically significant positive effect of facilitating conditions on behavioral intention (β = 0.351, p < 0.05), where FC acted as the second-strongest predictor of BI among UTAUT core variables. Xu and Zhang (2026), targeting Chinese university students’ academic use of DeepSeek, also validated a significant direct FC-to-BI relationship (β = 0.081, p < 0.05), albeit with a comparatively smaller effect size. We hypothesized that when students perceive sufficient hardware, learning resources, technical support, and assistance channels, their intention to use GenAI will significantly increase. In this study, trust in GenAI is defined as art students’ confidence in GenAI under conditions of uncertainty and risk regarding creative needs, originality, safety, fairness, and reliability. Students’ concerns extend far beyond functional efficiency at the tool level; they delve deeper into value-based issues such as the attribution of originality in AI-generated content, the potential risk of copyright infringement of existing works, and whether their artistic identity and creative autonomy are being eroded by algorithms (Ansone et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026). Precisely because of these unique concerns, trust plays a far more significant role in GenAI adoption decisions than in traditional information systems and is regarded by most scholars as the core psychological mechanism linking technological attributes to user behavior (Zhou et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025).

Metacognitive control refers to an individual’s capacity to strategically plan, continuously monitor, and flexibly adjust cognitive strategies while collaborating with GenAI on academic or creative-production tasks (Mahy and Li, 2026). This construct originates from the theoretical framework of self-regulated learning in cognitive psychology and includes four core dimensions (Mahy and Li, 2026): Planning: Prior to using GenAI, students formulate targeted interaction strategies according to task characteristics. Monitoring: During human–GenAI collaboration, students constantly evaluate whether AI outputs support the achievement of task goals. Regulation: In response to real-time feedback, students flexibly adjust interaction patterns to improve collaborative creative results. Role Awareness: Students explicitly clarify the division of responsibilities and boundary definitions between human creators and AI in collaborative creation.

The reason artistic creation requires more metacognitive control than information retrieval or data processing is not primarily because the tasks are “more difficult,” but because the evaluation criteria are more ambiguous, the stopping rules are less clear, and strategy shifts occur more frequently. Creative tasks are typically ill-defined and have no single correct answer; therefore, creators must continuously monitor their progress, adjust their strategies, and decide which ideas to retain, develop, or discard (Lebuda and Benedek, 2023). This means that creators must distinguish between the problem space and the solution space, and adjust their process according to the stage they are in; skipping a stage requires metacognitive reflection to identify and correct the issue (Von Thienen et al., 2023). Materials and methods

Study 1: survey study

Questionnaire design

This study employed a self-administered structured questionnaire that underwent multi-stage validation to ensure psychometric robustness and situational appropriateness. The questionnaire consisted of two parts, and all items measuring latent variables were adapted from established scales in the field of technology acceptance.

To ensure cross-linguistic equivalence, a standardized forward-backward translation procedure was adopted (Guillemin et al., 1993). Demographic questions and latent-variable measures appeared in separate survey modules to create psychological distance between predictor and outcome measures. An anonymity statement was prominently placed at the beginning of the questionnaire to reduce social desirability bias (Tehseen et al., 2017); all items were phrased in a neutral and concise manner, and the scale uniformly used a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).

The first section of the questionnaire collected four demographic characteristics: gender, major, educational attainment, and self-rated computer proficiency (Appendix Table A1); the second section measured seven core constructs comprising a total of 26 items, all adapted from well-validated scales and tailored to the context of artistic creation (Appendix Table A2) (Liu et al., 2015; Tarhini et al., 2017b; Birch and Irvine, 2009; Wrycza et al., 2017; Yao et al., 2022; Venkatesh et al., 2003; Zhu et al., 2025; Venkatesh et al., 2003; Cao et al., 2021; Mahy and Li, 2026; Chai et al., 2021).

Data collection

This study adopted a purposive sampling strategy, recruiting participants through an online survey. The inclusion criteria were as follows: enrollment in a regular higher education institution in Zhejiang Province, China; current student status in an art-and-design-related major; and prior experience in using generative artificial intelligence technology within their disciplinary studies.

Data were collected via the online questionnaire platform “Wenjuanxing” from April 1 to April 29, 2026. Questionnaire links were distributed by faculty collaborators at eight higher education institutions across Zhejiang Province, China, to students who met the inclusion criteria. After retrieval, rigorous data cleaning was performed: five invalid questionnaires were removed for excessively short completion time, identical responses across all items, or apparent logical contradictions. Consequently, 450 valid questionnaires were obtained, yielding a valid response rate of 98.9%.

As presented in Table 1, the overall Cronbach’s alpha for the entire questionnaire reached 0.927 (George and Mallery, 1999), indicating excellent internal consistency at the scale level. For the seven latent constructs, Cronbach’s alpha values ranged from 0.874 to 0.909. Study 2: experimental study

Rationale and research objectives

Study 2 used a between-subjects experiment to test whether the situational component of metacognitive control causally affect creative output. Study 1 established that MC is directly associated with behavioral intention and indirectly associated through trust. Study 2 does not test this mediation path; trust was not measured. Instead, it isolates the manipulable, situational component of MC, namely strategy prompts and scaffolds during AI-assisted creation, and examines its causal effect on creative quality and diversity. Study 2 thus supplements the MC to BI direct path identified in Study 1 with preliminary causal evidence, while operating at a different level: output quality rather than behavioral intention. The two studies use complementary triangulation. Together, they converge on the central role of metacognitive control in creative engagement, although they do so through different methods and at different outcome levels. Participants were recruited for homogeneous baseline characteristics and completed a standardized AI-generation task. Creative expression was decomposed into semantic content, visual style, and spatial composition.

Participants

All 80 participants were recruited from the valid sample of 450 art majors in Study 1. Study 1 respondents who met the inclusion criteria and consented to follow-up contact were invited to sign up voluntarily for a laboratory session, and enrollment was completed within the fixed 2-day window. Participants were then assigned to the metacognitive-control group (Group A; n = 40) or the control group (Group B; n = 40) by simple random assignment at a 1:1 ratio using a random number generator. Among them, 32 were male and 48 were female, aged 18–24 years (M = 20.35, SD = 1.27). All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision, had prior basic experience in using GenAI tools, and signed informed consent before the experiment. Baseline equivalence was verified across all baseline variables: baseline metacognitive-control score [t(78) = 0.18, p = 0.858], AI use experience (Mann–Whitney U = 788.00, p = 0.903), age [t(78) = 0.84, p = 0.405], and sex [χ2(1) = 0.00, p = 1.000]; no baseline variable differed significantly between groups (all p > 0.05). Because random assignment occurred after recruitment, self-selection is unlikely to have systematically biased the between-group comparison, although this cannot be entirely ruled out. At the same time, the voluntary nature of participation means that the sample may not fully represent the broader Study 1 population, which limits the external generalizability of the findings.

All participants used the same text-to-image generation model, Nano Banana 2 (official model name: Gemini 3.1 Flash Image), developed by Google DeepMind and released on February 26, 2026. The model was accessed through the Gemini app using the model identifier gemini-3.1-flash-image-preview. Because Nano Banana 2 is a preview model, it may be updated by the provider without notice. To ensure version stability, all image generation was performed in batches within a fixed two-day window (May 3–4, 2026). The two groups were distributed evenly across the 2 days (Day 1: 20 experimental and 21 control participants; Day 2: 20 experimental and 19 control), and the order of conditions was alternated so that no batch was composed of a single condition. Every batch used the identical model identifier and interface version, the same fixed output parameters (resolution 1 K, 1:1 aspect ratio, 15-min task window), and no custom fine-tuning, plug-ins, or parameter presets. The interface version and model identifier were recorded at the start of each session, and no model updates or interface changes were observed during the study period.

Nano Banana 2 was selected for three reasons. First, it offers high-fidelity image generation with strong instruction-following capability, which is essential for a standardized task in which all participants must generate an image based on the same keywords. Second, it supports high subject consistency and precise text rendering, reducing the likelihood that group differences are confounded by model failures or refusals. Third, it is freely available to Gemini users and provides fast generation speed, making it feasible for participants to complete multiple generation attempts within the 15-min window. Its improved natural language understanding allows the model to capture subtle differences in participants’ prompts, which is critical for detecting metacognitive-control effects on creative outcomes.

Experimental design and procedure

This study employed a one-factor between-subjects experimental design in which the independent variable was the presence versus absence of metacognitive control. The primary dependent variable was expert aesthetic evaluation of the submitted AI-assisted artworks across three dimensions: semantic content, visual style, and spatial composition. The secondary dependent variable was the within-group pairwise feature distance in the same three dimensions, computed using open-source models as an objective, auxiliary indicator of creative homogeneity. Participants were randomly assigned to the experimental group or the control group at a 1:1 ratio. Participants were kept blind to condition assignment, and all expert raters were blinded to group assignment. All experimental procedures were conducted in accordance with standardized laboratory protocols. The experiment was divided into four consecutive phases. In the baseline confirmation phase, participant identity was verified, informed consent was obtained, and standardized task instructions were provided. In the manipulation phase, participants in the experimental group received four-stage metacognitive prompts (Supplementary Table S1) prior to creation and were instructed to record their revised prompts afterward, whereas participants in the control group received only the standard task instructions and no metacognitive prompts. In the standardized AI-assisted creation task phase, all participants were required to use the Nano Banana 2 model with fixed parameters, an output resolution of 1K, and a 1:1 aspect ratio to generate one image within 15 min based on the keywords “balcony” and “cat,” and to submit one final AI-assisted artwork. In the outcome assessment phase, each submitted artwork was evaluated by three blinded experts and by machine-based feature-distance analysis.

The keywords “balcony” and “cat” were selected a priori for four reasons. First, they form a natural scene–subject combination: “balcony” specifies the setting, whereas “cat” specifies the main subject. This combination allows meaningful variation in semantic content, visual style, and spatial composition while keeping the task sufficiently constrained for a 15-min standardized creation task. Second, both words are concrete, familiar, and highly imageable, which reduces the influence of prior domain knowledge and vocabulary differences across participants. Prior research has established that imageability is positively correlated with the effectiveness of verbal cues in creative tasks (Johnson and Hass, 2022). Third, the combination is open-ended enough to permit diverse stylistic and compositional solutions (Oppenlaender, 2022), including realistic, illustrative, cinematic, minimalist, or fantasy approaches, as well as different camera angles, color palettes, and lighting conditions. Fourth, the keywords are neutral with respect to culture, profession, and sensitive content, and they avoid copyright or safety concerns that could trigger model refusals or filtering.

Expert aesthetic evaluation procedure

Expert aesthetic evaluation served as the primary outcome measure in Study 2. Three expert reviewers, blinded to group assignment, independently evaluated 80 AI-assisted artworks. Each artwork was scored on a 7-point Likert-type scale across three dimensions—semantic content, visual style, and spatial composition—according to the behavioral anchors specified in the Expert Review Form (Supplementary Documents). Reviewers were required to carefully read the review instructions and scoring criteria prior to evaluation to ensure consistent interpretation of the dimensions and anchors. Reviewers completed the ratings independently, were instructed not to discuss their scores, and were asked to base all judgments solely on direct observation of the artworks, without inferring author identity, creative process, or generation method. The expert rating scale was designed to assess aesthetic quality across semantic content, visual style, and spatial composition. It does not directly measure creativity or creative ability.

For each artwork, dimension scores were averaged across the three experts, and an overall aesthetic score was computed as the unweighted mean of all nine ratings. Inter-rater reliability was assessed using ICC(2,k) or Cronbach’s alpha. Group differences were tested using independent-samples t-tests with Welch correction, and Cohen’s d was reported as the effect size. Multiple comparisons across the three dimensions and the overall score were corrected using the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate procedure. All tests were two-tailed with α = 0.05. Accordingly, the study conclusions were derived from blinded expert aesthetic evaluations as the primary evidence, with machine-based feature distances serving only as a secondary, objective validation.

Machine-based feature extraction and comparison

All feature extraction and quantitative comparison procedures were implemented via self-developed offline Python scripts to eliminate subjective evaluation bias, with all pre-trained models loaded locally without online fine-tuning to guarantee reproducibility. To provide an objective, secondary validation of creative homogeneity, image features were extracted along three dimensions using open-source models. Semantic content representations were derived from an OpenCLIP ViT-B/32 image encoder, yielding a 512-dimensional embedding for each image. These embedding were L2-normalized, and pairwise content distance was operationalized as cosine distance, defined as 1 minus the cosine similarity between normalized embedding (Zhu et al., 2024). Visual style representations were obtained from an ImageNet-pretrained VGG19 network. Feature maps at indices 4, 9, 18, 27, and 36 of the torchvision VGG19 features module were used to compute layer-specific Gram matrices, which were flattened and concatenated into a single style vector. Pairwise style distances were computed using Euclidean distance (Sun et al., 2017). Spatial composition representations were derived from histogram of oriented gradients (HOG) descriptors. Each image was converted to grayscale, resized to 256 × 256 pixels, and represented by HOG features with 9 orientations, 32 × 32 pixels per cell, and 2 × 2 cells per block. Pairwise composition distances were calculated using Euclidean distance (Talaoubrid et al., 2022).

For each dimension (Table 6), a complete pairwise distance matrix was constructed across all images. Within-group mean distances were computed separately for the experimental group (A) and the control group (B), and the test statistic was defined as the difference between these means (A − B). Statistical significance was assessed using a strict permutation test with 10,000 permutations. Under the null hypothesis of no group effect, the group labels are exchangeable because participants were randomly assigned to the metacognitive prompting condition or the control condition, and the standardized task and model settings ensure that the generated images are otherwise comparable across groups. In each permutation, group labels were randomly reassigned while preserving the original group sizes, and the test statistic was recomputed, thereby maintaining the dependency structure of the full distance matrix. The two-sided p-value was computed as (b + 1) / (N + 1), where b denotes the number of permuted statistics with absolute values greater than or equal to the absolute observed statistic and N = 10,000. Bootstrap resampling with 10,000 replicates was performed within each group to estimate 95% confidence intervals for the difference using the percentile method. The permutation test provides a distribution-free p-value for the null hypothesis of no group difference, whereas the bootstrap confidence interval quantifies the uncertainty of the effect size estimate. Reporting both allows us to separate statistical significance from the precision of the estimated difference. Multiple comparisons across the three dimensions were corrected using the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate procedure. All analyses were implemented in Python with a fixed random seed of 42 to ensure reproducibility. Larger within-group distances indicate greater heterogeneity and, consequently, lower creative homogeneity. However, several objective limitations of the feature-distance metrics described above warrant caution. First, CLIP embedding, VGG19 Gram matrices, and HOG descriptors capture specific statistical properties—such as semantic embedding, texture statistics, and edge-gradient structures—and cannot fully represent the aesthetic and semantic richness of artistic content, style, and composition. Second, the within-group mean distance reflects the dispersion or heterogeneity of images in feature space and is not equivalent to creativity, creative quality, or aesthetic value. A larger distance may arise from greater randomness, generation noise, model artifacts, or stylistic drift rather than from more creative expression. Accordingly, these metrics serve only as an auxiliary objective validation of group differences in homogeneity; they cannot replace expert judgments of aesthetic quality and should not be used alone to infer that the experimental group is superior in creativity.

Experimental results

Inter-rater reliability and rater distributions. Inter-rater reliability was moderate across all expert-rated dimensions (Table 9). Because the inter-rater reliability was only moderate (ICC = 0.635–0.692), the between-group effect-size estimates carry non-trivial measurement error. The reported effect sizes, particularly d = 1.30 for visual style, should therefore be interpreted with caution; under reliability correction the underlying effect may be somewhat smaller than the observed estimate. The three raters showed comparable score distributions across dimensions (Supplementary Table S2). Levene’s test indicated no significant variance heterogeneity for any dimension (all p > 0.05). Because Welch’s t-test does not assume equal variances, it was used for all group comparisons. Expert aesthetic evaluation served as the primary outcome (Table 10). Group A (metacognitive control) significantly outperformed Group B (control) on all three dimensions. For semantic content, Group A (M = 5.02, SD = 0.60) scored significantly higher than Group B (M = 4.62, SD = 0.58). For visual style, Group A (M = 5.13, SD = 0.71) significantly exceeded Group B (M = 4.28, SD = 0.59). For spatial composition, Group A (M = 4.90, SD = 0.65) was significantly higher than Group B (M = 4.52, SD = 0.57). All differences remained significant after Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction, with the largest gain observed in visual style. As a robustness check (conducted post hoc), we additionally tested for batch effects by running a 2 (group) × 2 (session day) ANOVA on the expert-rated outcomes. No significant day × group interaction was found for Semantic content, F(1, 76) = 0.42, p = 0.519; Visual style, F(1, 76) = 0.01, p = 0.924; Spatial composition, F(1, 76) = 1.06, p = 0.308; or the overall score, F(1, 76) = 0.76, p = 0.386. The main effect of session day was also non-significant on all dimensions (all p > 0.05), and group differences remained significant after accounting for session day. These findings provide no evidence that session timing systematically confounded the group differences.

Discussion

Trust as the strongest correlate of behavioral intention

In Study 1, trust in GenAI showed the strongest direct association with behavioral intention (β = 0.425, p < 0.001). This finding differs from patterns observed in general educational technology research, where performance expectancy is typically regarded as the primary driver of behavioral intention. Students’ willingness to integrate GenAI into their creative processes was associated not only with expected gains in productivity but also, and in this sample more strongly, with perceived trustworthiness (Oc et al., 2024; Rana et al., 2025). The construct as operationalized here is primarily instrumental, supplemented by a modest art-value component. This strong association should not be read as evidence for a fully developed art-value trust dimension.

The role of trust was not uniform across paths in the model. For all five antecedents, the indirect association through trust was significant (bias-corrected 95% CIs excluded zero), and the direct association with behavioral intention remained significant after trust was included. This pattern is consistent with partial mediation for each antecedent. Substantively, partial mediation means that trust is not the sole pathway connecting these antecedents to behavioral intention. Each antecedent is associated with behavioral intention both through trust and through pathways that do not involve trust. For facilitating conditions, the direct association was small but significant (β = 0.092, p = 0.040; 10,000 bootstrap 95% CI [0.003, 0.179]). Thus, facilitating conditions are associated with behavioral intention partly through trust and partly through a direct association that is independent of trust. This direct association may reflect the possibility that resources, training, and support are associated with behavioral intention not only through their association with trust but also through their association with reduced perceived barriers to use. Because this direct association is close to the significance threshold, the partial mediation pattern should be interpreted cautiously. Overall, the mediation results suggest that trust is an important but not exhaustive explanatory pathway; the antecedents retain direct associations with behavioral intention that are independent of trust.

Social influence as the dominant correlate of trust

Among the five variables associated with trust, social influence had the highest standardized coefficient (β = 0.262, p < 0.001), and its indirect association with behavioral intention via trust was also the most pronounced among all indirect paths (indirect coefficient = 0.112), accounting for 42.1% of its total estimated association. In traditional information systems research, social influence is typically understood to operate through normative pressure or imitation mechanisms. However, in artistic creation contexts, its role may be more prominent because social influence may be closely tied to the standards used to evaluate the legitimacy of creative tools and outputs.

Artistic value is not objectively given but is constructed through social negotiation and institutional recognition (Wingström et al., 2024). When teachers, peers, and the broader arts community treat GenAI as a legitimate medium for artistic creation, students may perceive more than just social pressure to conform; they may update their normative beliefs about what constitutes authentic, masterful, and valuable artistic practice (Garcia, 2024; Wu et al., 2026). This socially constructed legitimacy may be closely linked to trust in the technology. The prominent role of social influence is thus consistent with the findings of other scholars’ qualitative studies, which suggest that art students’ attitudes toward AI are deeply embedded in community norms and the process of professional identity formation (Ursavaş et al., 2025). From a theoretical perspective, social influence may be more closely tied to students’ judgments of trust as a cognitive authority, rather than merely serving as a peripheral normative factor in this sample. The remaining three classic dimensions of the UTAUT model were significantly positively associated with trust in GenAI, all meeting the p < 0.001 criterion. While the strength of their associations with trust was slightly lower than that of social influence, together they may represent consistent technological and environmental correlates of trust. Educational attainment was significantly positively associated with behavioral intention (β = 0.072, p = 0.041). This pattern suggests that, in this sample, art students with higher educational attainment reported stronger behavioral intention to use GenAI.

Metacognitive control as a dual-path correlate of GenAI behavioral intention

In Study 1, metacognitive control was directly associated with behavioral intention (β = 0.146, p < 0.001) and was also associated with trust (β = 0.099, p = 0.042); the mediation results were consistent with an indirect association through trust. Taken together, this pattern is consistent with a dual-path process that may be involved in GenAI adoption in artistic contexts. This pattern suggests that metacognitive control may be associated with both greater trust in GenAI and greater willingness to use it.

This finding is consistent with the metacognitive framework for creativity proposed by other scholars, which suggests that metacognitive monitoring and regulation are important for managing the inherent ambiguity and openness of creative tasks (Lebuda and Benedek, 2023). Unlike structured problem-solving tasks with clear termination rules, artistic creation often requires continuous evaluation of whether the output is sufficiently original, aesthetically coherent, and aligned with the creator’s intent (Green et al., 2023). Study 2 results converge with the survey findings on the role of metacognitive control. The pronounced association with visual style suggests that situational metacognitive guidance may be particularly relevant for outputs that deviate from the model’s default stylistic tendencies. However, this should be interpreted as greater output diversity within the feature space, not as direct evidence of enhanced creativity. It should be noted that these effect magnitudes are obtained within a tightly-controlled short-term laboratory setting and may shrink when transferred to authentic classroom contexts. Regarding computational feature-distance outcomes, larger within-group pairwise distances reflect higher heterogeneity among generated images within each experimental group. This metric captures statistical dispersion in semantic embedding, texture-style statistics, and edge-based compositional structure rather than artistic merit. The convergent pattern between expert quality ratings and computational dispersion offers supplementary evidence that metacognitive prompting may be associated with higher expert-rated aesthetic quality and greater output heterogeneity. However, computational diversity alone cannot stand as a proxy for creative quality, and the expert rating scale assesses aesthetic quality rather than creativity itself. Machine-based within-group feature-distance analyses converged in direction: Group A showed greater within-group diversity than Group B across all three dimensions. These findings provide preliminary experimental evidence that, under the conditions examined, metacognitive prompting relative to no prompting is associated with higher expert-rated aesthetic quality and greater output diversity. Theoretically, Study 2 frames situational metacognitive prompting both as a complement to the self-reported individual-difference construct of metacognitive control and as a situational factor amenable to instructional support. This framing carries direct practical implications: because metacognitive prompts can be embedded in educational practice at minimal cost, they may help students engage more actively with GenAI rather than passively accept its outputs. However, Study 2’s conclusions are subject to important boundary conditions. It manipulated situational metacognitive prompts, not the stable construct of metacognitive control; it did not measure trust or test the mediating pathway proposed in Study 1 or the full theoretical model. Moreover, the computational indicators capture specific statistical properties and should not be equated with creativity or aesthetic value; expert ratings therefore serve as the primary evidence. The results are also limited to a short-term task, specific keywords, one image-generation model, fixed parameter settings, and Chinese art students in higher education institutions in Zhejiang Province. Thus, Study 2 should be read as providing complementary and preliminary experimental evidence for one component of the proposed process, not as resolving the GenAI creativity paradox or demonstrating the full mechanism.

From correlates to practice: cultivating trust and metacognitive control in GenAI-supported art education

Given that Study 1 identifies trust and social influence as strongly associated predictors, arts educators serve as role models who shape perceptions of legitimate artistic practice within studio-based learning contexts (Hamblen, 1985). Social influence in art education extends beyond superficial peer pressure: teachers’ attitudes, feedback styles, and framing of GenAI are associated with students’ professional-identity formation and their value-based judgments about authentic artistic creation. Teacher development programs should prioritize training educators not only in the technical skills required to use GenAI tools but also in teaching strategies designed to help students engage with AI in critical, reflective, and creative ways (Le et al., 2026). Drawing on practice-based pedagogy, the integration of AI-enhanced critique, human-machine collaborative projects, and explicit discussions of authorship and originality can help establish GenAI as a legitimate creative medium while maintaining rigorous artistic standards (Jiang et al., 2026). Such classroom dialogues should address the dimensions of trust related to artistic ethics covered by the scale used in this study—namely, attribution of originality, algorithmic fairness, and respect for creative safety—rather than being limited solely to instrumental performance expectations.

Findings from Study 2 indicate that beyond technical-skill instruction, course designers should integrate metacognitive-control training. Suitable activities include reflective journals documenting collaborative workflows, iterative-focused structured prompt-design tasks, and group discussions on role boundaries. Teaching only prompt-engineering tricks and tool operations cannot fully address risks associated with students passively adopting formulaic algorithm-generated outputs. Curriculum designers may integrate metacognitive-control training into GenAI-infused art courses around the four intervention dimensions: planning, monitoring, regulation, and human-AI role awareness. Practical instructional activities include structured prompt-design worksheets to articulate pre-generation creative goals; iterative-revision logs documenting prompt adjustments based on AI outputs; comparative critique tasks contrasting raw AI outputs with human-refined versions; and post-creation reflective journals that demarcate human creative decisions from algorithmic contributions. For assessment, instructors may assign greater weight to metacognitive process documentation, including creative planning, iterative revisions, and critical evaluation of AI outputs, rather than grading solely on the aesthetic polish of final generated images.

It should be emphasized that these experimental effects were observed within a short-term, controlled laboratory task with fixed keywords and a single image-generation model, which limits the generalizability of results. The metacognitive-prompt template should be treated as a flexible pedagogical scaffold instead of a universal checklist. For open-ended, complex studio assignments in real-world classrooms, educators can adapt and simplify the four-stage prompts according to project demands and student proficiency levels.

Conclusion and limitations

Research conclusion

This study explores psychological predictors of art students’ GenAI behavioral intentions within higher art education. Drawing on cross-sectional survey structural equation modeling analysis and controlled laboratory experiments, this paper extends the UTAUT framework to artistic creation contexts. The trust construct operationalized in this research builds upon rather than replaces conventional technology trust. Instead, it builds upon foundational instrumental trust concerning system stability, operational reliability and data security, and further incorporates domain-specific value-related concerns unique to art practice, including perceptions of output originality, authorship attribution, and algorithmic fairness.

Empirical results indicate that trust in the GenAI construct is the strongest direct predictor of students’ behavioral intention to use GenAI for creation. Classic UTAUT antecedents were associated with behavioral intention both directly and indirectly through trust. Among these predictors, social influence correlates most strongly with trust in GenAI. Within artistic contexts, social influence is not limited to normative peer pressure; it corresponds to community- and institution-based evaluations that may inform students’ perceptions of both the technical dependability and artistic-ethical appropriateness of AI-assisted creation.

Metacognitive control shows dual associations with behavioral intention: it is positively associated with behavioral intention directly, and it is also positively associated with trust in GenAI. When learners deploy metacognitive strategies including planning, monitoring, regulation, and clear awareness of human-AI role boundaries, they can better assess system performance and identify potential value-related risks such as copyright ambiguities. Experimental findings show that situational metacognitive support is associated with higher expert-rated aesthetic quality and greater output diversity across semantic content, visual style, and spatial composition.

The present data offer limited preliminary experimental evidence. Even technically stable GenAI systems may yield formulaic outputs under passive user engagement. The current results are consistent with the possibility that metacognitive control may be associated with reduced tendencies toward formulaic outputs, though these observations should be interpreted cautiously given laboratory constraints.

From a practical standpoint, art educators should recognize the dual composition of GenAI-related trust. Instruction should support students to first develop confidence in basic system functions, while also encouraging deliberate reflection on art-specific value considerations such as originality and authorship. The extended UTAUT model integrating instrumental and domain-specific value-based trust provides an empirically grounded reference for subsequent technology-acceptance research in creative education settings.

Limitations and future directions

Several limitations constrain the interpretation of study findings. First, survey data are cross-sectional. While the experiment identifies effects of situational metacognitive prompts on creative outputs, cross-sectional data cannot establish definitive temporal ordering or causal direction among metacognitive control, trust in GenAI, and behavioral intention.

Second, participants are Chinese art-major students sampled exclusively from Zhejiang Province. Cultural understandings of artistic authorship, institutional AI policies, and baseline expectations for technical-system trust differ across regions and disciplines. Such contextual factors may change the relative weight of instrumental trust versus art-value-aligned trust within the overall trust construct.

Third, the laboratory experiment adopts short-term, constrained creation tasks with fixed keywords and a single GenAI model. Authentic studio assignments feature open-ended themes and long iterative cycles. Observed output-diversity improvements under laboratory conditions may not fully generalize to real-world classroom practice. In addition, computational feature-distance metrics only capture statistical dispersion of image features; they cannot serve as comprehensive proxies for artistic creativity or nuanced subjective value-based trust perceptions.

Fourth, the present design cannot test the GenAI creativity paradox itself. The paradox concerns declining collective-level novelty across independent users of a shared model (Doshi and Hauser, 2024), whereas Study 2 measured within-group output dispersion under a single model. Directly testing the paradox would require multiple groups of participants who share the same model and task, with the collective-level distribution of outputs measured and compared across conditions.

Fifth, a measurement limitation should be acknowledged. Because the two authorship items that formed a separate factor were removed in the EFA, and only two of the five retained items (TI2 and TI4) capture art-specific value concerns, the trust scale used here predominantly measures instrumental technology trust and only partially covers the art-value dimension. Consequently, the present findings should be read as concerning a primarily instrumental trust construct, and a dedicated, validated trust scale for art-specific AI contexts is needed in future research to more fully capture value-laden trust.

Based on these constraints, several directions are suggested for future research. Longitudinal research can track dynamic shifts in instrumental trust, art-specific value-based trust, metacognitive strategies and adoption behaviors as students accumulate ongoing AI co-creation experience. Such designs may help examine whether instrumental trust acts as a precondition for the development of art-oriented value-based trust. Cross-cultural and cross-disciplinary replications are needed to test model external validity. Researchers can explore how cultural and institutional contexts alter the relative salience of instrumental trust and domain-specific value-based trust across fine arts, design, media arts and non-art disciplines.

Follow-up experimental work may further separate and examine the two sub-components of trust. It remains to be tested whether metacognitive interventions exert differential influences on instrumental system trust versus art-specific value-based trust, and whether trust mediates the link between metacognitive prompting and creative outcomes.

Field-based intervention research embedded within real art curricula is also warranted. Curriculum modules may be designed to foster baseline system trust, facilitate critical reflection on art-related value dilemmas, and deliver metacognitive-control training. Further work may develop assessment approaches that balance technical proficiency, documentation of metacognitive processes, and critical reflection on authorship and algorithm-related ethical issues. Mixed-methods research combining quantitative scales and qualitative interviews can advance understanding of how art students navigate tensions between tool performance and artistic-value considerations during human-AI collaborative creation.

articles.title: A meta-analysis of the effects of aerobic exercise on inhibitory control in university students and an analysis of moderating effects
articles.author: Shaofeng Peng
articles.summary:
Background

Aerobic exercise has been increasingly recognized as a potential strategy for enhancing executive function, yet its effect on inhibitory control in university students remains inconsistent, and the intervention characteristics associated with effect variability are unclear. This meta-analysis aimed to synthesize randomized controlled trial evidence on the effects of aerobic exercise on inhibitory control in university students and to explore potential moderators.

Methods

PubMed, PsycARTICLES, PsycINFO, ScienceDirect, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, CNKI, Wanfang, and VIP were systematically searched from inception to March 2026. Randomized controlled trials involving university students aged 18–25 years, aerobic exercise interventions, eligible control conditions, and validated inhibitory-control tasks were included. Hedges’ g was used as the effect-size metric. Random-effects models with restricted maximum likelihood estimation and Hartung–Knapp adjustment were applied. Subgroup analyses examined participant type, intervention period, exercise intensity, exercise session duration, and task paradigm, and exploratory univariable multilevel meta-regression was conducted to account for multiple effects nested within studies.

Results

Nine independent studies involving 605 participants were included. Aerobic exercise produced a small but statistically significant improvement in inhibitory control (Hedges’ g = −0.353, 95% CI [−0.591, −0.115], p = 0.009), with low statistical heterogeneity (I2 = 26.98%). Leave-one-study-out analyses showed stable pooled estimates (g = −0.397 to −0.288). No statistically significant between-group differences were observed for participant type, intervention period, exercise intensity, exercise session duration, or task paradigm. Exploratory meta-regression likewise identified no statistically significant moderator associations. Egger’s test was not significant (p = 0.072).

Conclusion

Aerobic exercise may produce a small but statistically significant improvement in inhibitory control among university students; however, the practical significance of this effect remains uncertain, and the current evidence is entirely based on studies conducted in China. Although some intervention subgroups showed numerically different effect estimates, the limited number of independent studies means that the current evidence is insufficient to determine whether participant or exercise characteristics moderate the intervention effect. Further high-quality randomized trials are needed to clarify dose–response relationships and optimize aerobic exercise prescriptions for inhibitory-control enhancement.

Systematic Review Registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261335563. CRD420261335563).

1

Introduction

In a complex information environment, an individual’s capacity for self-control is particularly crucial. Inhibitory control, a key component of executive function, refers to an individual’s ability to suppress dominant responses, resist distracting stimuli, and regulate their behaviour, cognition and emotional responses in accordance with goal requirements (Diamond, 2013; Lee et al., 2025; Sosa, 2024). Executive function, as a vital higher-order cognitive process that underpins goal-directed behaviour, comprises three core components: inhibitory control, working memory and cognitive flexibility. It plays a crucial role in information processing, behavioural regulation and decision-making within complex environments (Badre, 2025; Diamond, 2013; Tervo-Clemmens et al., 2023; Yanguez et al., 2024). As a key demographic in the stage of ongoing cognitive development and the shaping of behavioural patterns, university students need to rely on sound inhibitory control to regulate emotional and behavioural responses, resist immediate temptations, and maintain goal-directed behaviour and the pursuit of long-term goals (Inzlicht et al., 2021; Luciana and Collins, 2022; Tervo-Clemmens et al., 2023; Werner and Berkman, 2024). However, as the information environment becomes more complex, academic pressures increase and lifestyles change, the cognitive control abilities of university students are receiving increasing attention (Belluardo et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2020; McGrath et al., 2023). Therefore, exploring effective strategies to enhance inhibitory control in university students is of great significance for optimising cognitive performance and promoting mental health.

As a safe, cost-effective and easily implementable non-pharmacological intervention, aerobic exercise has attracted widespread attention in recent years for its role in enhancing cognitive function (Chang et al., 2025; Ishihara et al., 2021; Singh et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2024). Existing research suggests that aerobic exercise may influence higher-order cognitive processing through mechanisms such as increasing cerebral blood flow, promoting the release of neurotrophic factors, and modulating prefrontal cortex-related neural activity (Byun et al., 2014; Moreau and Chapple-De Lange, 2026; Tomoto et al., 2023). Previous research has shown that the cognitive effects of exercise are not limited to the domain of executive function; previous systematic reviews and meta-analyses suggest that exercise may also influence memory function, and that the effects of acute exercise on episodic memory may be influenced by factors such as the temporal relationship between exercise and memory tasks (Loprinzi et al., 2019; Loprinzi et al., 2018). In particular, inhibitory control relies on the prefrontal cortex and associated executive control networks, and the relationship between these functions and exercise-induced physiological and neural changes has also attracted considerable attention (Friedman and Robbins, 2022; Ishihara et al., 2021). Consequently, the impact of aerobic exercise on inhibitory control has gradually attracted attention in the field of exercise cognition.

In recent years, a large number of experimental studies have examined the effects of aerobic exercise on inhibitory control in university students, using classic cognitive paradigms such as the Stroop task, the Flanker task and the Go/No-go task (Ishihara et al., 2021; Li et al., 2025; Remiszewski et al., 2025). Some studies have found that acute aerobic exercise can enhance an individual’s efficiency in processing conflicting information, as evidenced by shorter reaction times or lower error rates (Chang et al., 2025; Kujach et al., 2018). Long-term aerobic exercise interventions have also been found to potentially improve an individual’s response inhibition and interference suppression abilities. For example, several studies involving acute exercise trials at different intensities have found that moderate-intensity aerobic exercise may produce a more pronounced enhancement of inhibitory control than low- or high-intensity exercise, suggesting that exercise intensity may influence the relationship between physical activity and cognitive performance (Kujach et al., 2018). Furthermore, long-term exercise intervention studies have also shown that regular aerobic exercise may improve inhibitory control in specific groups, such as university students with internet or smartphone addiction (Nie and Fan, 2025; Wang and Li, 2025). However, not all studies have observed consistent positive effects; some studies have found that performance on inhibitory tasks did not show significant improvement following aerobic exercise interventions (Ciria et al., 2018; Ishihara et al., 2021; Kao et al., 2022).

These inconsistent findings suggest that the effects of aerobic exercise on inhibitory control may exhibit some heterogeneity. The underlying causes of these differences may be related to the characteristics of the exercise interventions and the characteristics of the participants (Ishihara et al., 2021; Ludyga et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2026). On the one hand, aerobic exercise is not a single form of intervention; its effects may be influenced by factors such as exercise intensity, type of exercise, duration of the intervention, exercise session duration, and total exercise volume. On the other hand, individual differences—such as age, gender, baseline physical activity levels, and cognitive status—may also influence the cognitive adaptation process following exercise intervention. However, existing research has largely focused on testing effects under single experimental conditions, and there remains a lack of systematic analysis regarding how different intervention parameters and individual characteristics modulate the impact of aerobic exercise on inhibitory control.

To date, meta-analyses have examined the relationship between exercise and executive function from various perspectives. For example, Ishihara et al. (2021) conducted a meta-analysis of individual participant data on the effects of acute aerobic exercise on executive function, whilst Dkaidek et al. (2023) further investigated the impact of a single session of power cycling on executive function in young adults. Recently, Zhang et al. (2026) conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of exercise interventions and executive function in university students, reporting effects on inhibitory control, working memory and cognitive flexibility, respectively. However, there remain significant differences between existing meta-analyses and the research focus of this study. Ishihara et al. focused primarily on a single session of acute aerobic exercise and were therefore unable to address the effects of long-term aerobic training on inhibitory control (Ishihara et al., 2021; Dkaidek et al., 2023) further restricted the intervention to a single session of high-power cycling, and their conclusions are likewise primarily applicable to acute exercise scenarios. Although Zhang et al. included both acute and long-term exercise and reported the effects on inhibitory control separately, their overall research framework encompassed a variety of exercise forms—including aerobic exercise, high-intensity interval training, resistance training, Tai Chi, jumping and Tabata—whilst examining three components of executive function: inhibitory control, working memory and cognitive flexibility. Consequently, their analysis of the specific relationship between “aerobic exercise and inhibitory control” remains primarily a component of a broader exercise–executive function framework (Zhang et al., 2026). Furthermore, Zhang et al. (2026) examination of factors such as exercise type, intensity, session duration and intervention period was conducted primarily through subgroup analyses, without further employing meta-regression to test the associations between these potential moderators and the effect sizes. It is therefore still necessary to further restrict the intervention type to aerobic exercise and the outcome to inhibitory control, and, based on a unified definition of effect size, to further examine the relationship between exercise intensity, intervention period, exercise session duration, participant type and task paradigm, and differences in intervention effects.

On this basis, this study further focuses on aerobic exercise as a specific form of intervention and inhibitory control as a specific component of executive function. It includes only randomised controlled trials and uses meta-analysis to comprehensively evaluate the overall effect of aerobic exercise on inhibitory control in university students. Furthermore, methods such as exploratory subgroup analysis and univariate multilevel meta-regression are employed to examine the relationship between exercise intensity, intervention period, exercise session duration, participant type and task paradigm with variations in the observed effects. The aim is to provide more targeted quantitative evidence building on existing research into exercise and executive function, and to offer guidance for the development of cognitive enhancement programmes and the implementation of exercise interventions for university students.

2

Methods

This study conducted its literature search in strict accordance with the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses and the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines (registration number: CRD420261335563).

2.1

Literature search

A search was conducted for Chinese and English literature published both domestically and internationally, covering the period from the inception of each database to March 2026. The literature search employed a combination of subject headings and free-text terms; the English search terms primarily included terms related to the study population, such as “students” OR “young adult” OR “college student” OR “university student” OR “undergraduate,” terms related to the intervention, such as “exercise” OR “aerobic exercise” OR “aerobic” OR “endurance” OR “running” OR “cycling” OR “swimming” OR “walking,” and terms related to outcome measures, such as “cognition” OR “executive function” OR “inhibitory control.” Searches were conducted in foreign-language databases such as PubMed, PsycARTICLES, PsycINFO, ScienceDirect, Web of Science and the Cochrane Library. Chinese literature was primarily retrieved from CNKI, Wanfang Database and VIP Database, using search terms including “students OR university students OR young people OR undergraduates OR higher education students,” “aerobic exercise OR aerobic training OR exercise intervention OR endurance training OR cycling OR jogging OR walking OR swimming,” and “cognitive function OR executive function OR inhibitory control.” Additionally, a back-search was conducted on the references of the included studies and relevant reviews to enhance the comprehensiveness of the literature search. The initial search was conducted in January 2026, with an updated search carried out in March 2026.

2.2

Inclusion and exclusion criteria

2.2.1

Inclusion criteria

Population: The study included university students aged between 18 and 25, regardless of gender. The age range was restricted to 18–25 in order to focus on young university students at a relatively consistent stage of development and to minimise the heterogeneity in developmental stages that a wider age range might entail; this age range corresponds to the classic core age range of ‘emerging adulthood’ (Arnett, 2000). Intervention: The experimental group receives an aerobic exercise intervention, comprising typical forms of aerobic exercise such as running, cycling, swimming and walking; the study must clearly report relevant information such as exercise intensity, duration of each session, frequency of exercise and duration of the intervention. Comparison: The control group receives no exercise intervention, engages in routine physical activity or is placed on a waiting list. Outcome Measures: Assessment must be based on at least one classic inhibitory control task, including the Stroop task, the Flanker task or the Go/No-go task; data metrics suitable for calculating effect sizes (such as mean, standard deviation and sample size) must be reported. Study Design: Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) are included.

2.2.2

Exclusion criteria

Reviews, meta-analyses, animal studies, case reports, cross-sectional studies, cohort studies and non-randomised experimental studies. Studies in which the study population did not consist of university students, or from which data on university students could not be extracted separately. Studies with incomplete data from which effect sizes could not be calculated. Duplicate publications. Literature for which the full text could not be obtained or from which valid research data could not be extracted.

2.3

Selection of literature and data extraction

The retrieved literature was first de-duplicated using literature management software; subsequently, two researchers independently carried out title and abstract screening, full-text assessment, data extraction and coding in accordance with pre-defined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Where discrepancies arose, these were resolved through discussion or by consulting a third-party researcher until consensus was reached (Guimarães et al., 2022; Page et al., 2021). The data extracted from the studies primarily included the first author, year of publication, study location, sample size, basic characteristics of the study participants, exercise intervention protocol (type of exercise, exercise intensity, exercise frequency, duration of each session and duration of the intervention), control conditions, type of inhibitory control task and relevant statistical data. The specific coding details are shown in Table 1.
