2.4

Assessment of the quality of the included studies

Two researchers assessed the included studies using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool, which covers five domains: the randomisation process, deviation from the intended intervention, missing outcome data, outcome measurement, and selective reporting of results; the overall risk of bias was categorised as “Low risk,” “Some concerns” or “High risk” (Sterne et al., 2019).

2.5

Calculation of the effect size

This study employed Hedges’ g, calculated as the standardised mean difference, as the effect size measure to reduce bias in effect size estimates under small-sample conditions (Nakamura, 2026; Suero et al., 2023). Effect sizes were calculated using Comprehensive Meta-Analysis Version 3.3 (CMA 3.3) software. For randomised controlled trials employing a pre-test–post-test design, the primary analysis calculated the standardised mean difference between the intervention and control groups based on the post-test means, standard deviations and sample sizes at the end of the intervention, and further applied small-sample correction to obtain Hedges’ g. To ensure consistency in the definition of effect sizes across different studies, the primary analysis employed a uniform post-test between-group comparison method, rather than a mixed approach using change scores or effect estimates adjusted for covariates. Baseline data were primarily used to assess the comparability of the experimental and control groups prior to the intervention and were not directly included in the calculation of the primary effect size.

This study draws upon Cohen’s classic criteria for evaluating effect sizes, using 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8 as the thresholds for small, medium and large effect sizes, respectively, (Andrade, 2020). With regard to the coding of effect size direction, the direction of performance improvement was first determined based on the definitions of each outcome measure in the original study. The inhibitory control measures used in the main analysis were all reaction times or conflict/interference measures calculated from reaction times. For measures where a decrease in score indicates improved inhibitory control performance, the effect size was calculated based on the raw between-group difference between the experimental and control groups; if the scoring direction of the original measure was opposite to the unified effect direction, the sign of the effect size was reversed. Once the direction was unified, a value of Hedges’ g < 0 indicated that the aerobic exercise group performed better in inhibitory control than the control group, whilst a value of Hedges’ g > 0 indicated that the control group performed better. Overall and subgroup effects were analysed using a random-effects model with REML estimation, and 95% confidence intervals and significance levels were calculated using the Hartung–Knapp method (Langan et al., 2019; van Aert and Jackson, 2019). Heterogeneity between studies was assessed using Cochran’s Q statistic, the I2 statistic and the estimate of between-study variance (τ2), with τ2 estimated using the REML method. It is generally accepted that I2 values of 25%, 50 and 75% represent low, moderate and high levels of heterogeneity, respectively (Cordero and Dans, 2021).

For multi-arm randomised controlled trials comprising multiple intervention arms that meet the inclusion criteria and share the same control group, this study was conducted in accordance with the methodological recommendations for Cochrane systematic reviews (Rücker et al., 2017). Where multiple intervention arms are clinically and methodologically homogeneous, they are combined into a single intervention arm for comparison with the shared control arm; the pooled sample size is the sum of the sample sizes of the individual intervention arms, the pooled mean is calculated using sample size weighting, and the pooled standard deviation is calculated using the formula recommended in the Cochrane Handbook. For moderator analyses requiring the retention of information from different intervention arms—such as those concerning exercise intensity—the individual intervention arms are retained, and the sample size of the shared control group is split according to the number of included intervention arms, whilst the mean and standard deviation of the control group remain unchanged (Rücker et al., 2017). This procedure is used to avoid repeated weighting of the same control participants and the resulting unit-of-analysis problem; however, it does not make the resulting effect-size comparisons statistically independent. In multilevel meta-regression analyses, multiple effect sizes from the same study are therefore nested within the study to account for their within-study dependence (Fernández-Castilla et al., 2020). In the analysis of overall effects, multiple intervention arms that are clinically and methodologically homogeneous are pooled to avoid double-counting of the shared control group; however, for moderating analyses—such as those involving exercise intensity—where information on the different intervention arms needs to be retained, each arm is retained separately to examine the relationship between different intervention characteristics and the effect size. Details of the specific outcome measures, post-test data and information on effect size calculations for each study included in the primary analysis are set out in Supplementary Table S1.

2.6

Assessment of publication bias and sensitivity analysis

A preliminary assessment of potential publication bias was conducted using funnel plots and the fail-safe number (Nfs), and publication bias was further tested using Egger’s linear regression method (Sterne et al., 2011). At the same time, sensitivity analyses were conducted by sequentially excluding individual studies to examine the impact of each study on the overall effect size and the stability of the study conclusions (Kunze et al., 2023). In addition, sensitivity analyses were conducted on studies assessed as high risk for overall bias to examine the impact of study quality on the estimates of the overall effect.

2.7

Analysis of moderating factors

To further investigate the potential sources of heterogeneity in the effects of aerobic exercise interventions, this study, drawing on existing theoretical foundations and a pre-defined coding scheme, identified participant type, intervention period, exercise intensity, exercise session duration and task paradigm as potential moderator variables (Page et al., 2021). In this study, participants were categorised into the general population and specific groups; the specific groups comprised a sample of university students specifically recruited on the basis of characteristics such as overweight, internet or smartphone addiction, or symptoms of depression. The intervention period was classified according to duration into single acute exercise sessions and long-term exercise training programmes lasting several weeks. In this study, the exercise session duration refers to the actual duration of each training session or single acute exercise session, as distinct from the intervention period, which denotes the overall duration of the intervention. Given the differences between the two types of intervention in terms of time scale and potential mechanisms of action, in addition to the overall combined analysis, a sensitivity analysis was conducted that included only studies on long-term exercise training to examine whether the overall effect estimate was influenced by studies on acute exercise.

Exercise intensity was standardised using a hierarchical coding principle. Firstly, if the original study explicitly reported that the intervention was of moderate or high intensity, the intensity classification from the original study was prioritised; if the original study did not explicitly specify the intensity category, coding was performed based on the reported physiological or subjective load indicators, with reference to the relative exercise intensity standards of the American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM). Moderate intensity is typically defined as 40–59% of heart rate reserve (HRR) or oxygen consumption reserve (VO₂R), 64–76% of maximum heart rate (HRmax), 46–63% of maximum oxygen consumption (VO₂max), or a Borg 6–20 scale RPE of 12–13; High intensity is typically defined as 60–89% of HRR or VO₂R, 77–95% of HRmax, 64–90% of VO₂max, or an RPE of 14–17 on the Borg scale; For studies reporting target intensity ranges that span adjacent categories or employ variable-intensity or interval training protocols, coding is based on the original study’s definition of intervention intensity and the target intensity for the main exercise phases (Garber et al., 2011; Huang et al., 2026).

The exercise session duration was categorised into two groups— ≤30 min and >30 min—using a 30-min threshold, based on the stratification method employed in previous systematic reviews and meta-analyses examining the association between exercise and executive function (Zhang et al., 2026).

For categorical variables, subgroup analyses were conducted to compare differences in effect sizes across different study characteristics. Given the limited number of included independent studies, and to reduce the risk of overfitting and unstable regression coefficients in multivariate models, the meta-regression employed an exploratory univariate analysis strategy. Specifically, independent multilevel random-effects meta-regression models were established separately for participant type, intervention period, exercise intensity, exercise session duration, and task paradigm, rather than including multiple moderator variables simultaneously within a single model (Higgins and Thompson, 2004). Where a single study contributed multiple effect sizes, these were nested within the study to account for the interdependence of effect sizes within that study (Fernández-Castilla et al., 2020). Given the limited number of independent studies, all meta-regression results are interpreted as exploratory findings.

3.1

Inclusion and coding of literature

The literature screening process is illustrated in Figure 1. Following database searches, literature screening and full-text evaluation, nine articles meeting the inclusion criteria were ultimately included. These comprised nine independent studies with a total sample size of 605 participants (Gao et al., 2025; Li et al., 2020; Nie and Fan, 2025; Si et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2023; Yang and He, 2023; Yu, 2023a, 2023b; Zhang et al., 2017). Of these, nine studies were conducted in China and none abroad. All included studies employed a randomised controlled trial design, with the study participants primarily comprising university students aged 18–25. The types of studies included acute aerobic exercise interventions and long-term exercise interventions. Based on participant characteristics, the included studies comprised both general university student populations and university student populations with specific characteristics. Among these, four studies involving special populations, totalling 321 participants, included overweight university students, university students with internet addiction, and university students with depressive symptoms; five studies involving general university students, totalling 284 participants, were also included. Interventions primarily comprised swimming, running, stationary cycling, aerobics and comprehensive aerobic exercise programmes, whilst the assessment tasks mainly included the Stroop task and the Flanker task. One study reported follow-up measurements, with a follow-up period exceeding 6 weeks. Quality assessment was conducted using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool 2.0. Among the included studies, none were classified as having a low risk of bias; seven were classified as having some concerns; and two were classified as having a high risk of bias. 3.2

The effect of aerobic exercise on inhibitory control in university students

The nine included studies comprised a total of nine independent research projects. A meta-analysis using a random-effects model was conducted to assess the overall effect of aerobic exercise interventions on inhibitory control in university students. The results indicated that aerobic exercise significantly improved inhibitory control in university students (g = −0.353, 95% CI: −0.591 to −0.115, p = 0.009), with the overall effect size reaching the level of a small effect. As the direction of the effect size was standardised in this study—with a negative value indicating that the exercise intervention group performed better in terms of inhibitory control than the control group—these results suggest that aerobic exercise can, to a certain extent, improve inhibitory control performance in university students. The results of the heterogeneity test indicated that there was low statistical heterogeneity in the effect sizes (Q = 10.96, df = 8, I2 = 26.98 per cent, τ2 = 0.012). Further sensitivity analysis revealed that, upon sequentially excluding individual studies, the pooled effect size ranged from g = −0.397 to −0.288; the direction of the effect remained unchanged in all cases and was statistically significant in each instance, indicating that the overall results are reasonably robust. Furthermore, given the differences in intervention period between single-session acute exercise and long-term exercise training, two studies involving single-session acute exercise were further excluded, and only seven long-term exercise training studies were included in the sensitivity analysis. The results showed that the pooled effect in the sensitivity analysis restricted to long-term training was g = −0.331 (95% CI: −0.662 to 0.001, p = 0.050), with between-study heterogeneity of I2 = 40.93% (Q = 10.16, τ2 = 0.041). The direction and magnitude of this effect were similar to those of the overall analysis, although the 95% confidence interval straddled 0 slightly. After further excluding two studies with a high overall risk of bias, the pooled effect of the remaining seven studies was g = −0.383 (95% CI: −0.729 to −0.037, p = 0.035), with I2 = 43.55% and τ2 = 0.053; the direction and magnitude of the effect were essentially consistent with those of the overall analysis. The results of the publication bias test showed that the Egger linear regression test did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.072), with a fail-safe number (Nfs) of 138; however, given the small number of included studies, the statistical power of the Egger test is limited, and therefore the possibility of publication bias or the small-sample effect cannot be ruled out on this basis. 3.3

Subgroup analysis of the effects of aerobic exercise interventions

Building on the existing research literature and the characteristics of the included studies, this study conducted exploratory subgroup analyses of factors that may influence the effects of aerobic exercise interventions. The results of the subgroup analysis showed that the direction of the effect was favourable to the aerobic exercise group across different participant types, intervention periods, exercise intensities, exercise session durations and task paradigms. 4

Discussion

This meta-analysis synthesised evidence from randomised controlled trials examining the effects of aerobic exercise on inhibitory control in university students. Compared with no exercise intervention, routine activity or a waiting list control, aerobic exercise demonstrated a small but statistically significant improvement in inhibitory control among university students (g = −0.353, 95% CI: −0.591 to −0.115, p = 0.009). However, this effect is generally of modest magnitude, and as existing studies have primarily utilised laboratory-based inhibitory control tasks such as the Stroop and Flanker tests for evaluation, it remains to be verified whether this can be further translated into practical improvements in learning, self-regulation or other aspects of daily functioning. The statistical heterogeneity of the overall effect size was low, and neither the direction of the effect nor its statistical significance changed when individual studies were excluded one by one, indicating that the overall results possess a certain degree of stability. At the same time, the low I2 value merely reflects the relatively limited statistical heterogeneity observed among the effect sizes; it does not imply that the included studies are highly homogeneous in terms of clinical and methodological characteristics. Overall, this study focuses specifically on the executive function component of inhibitory control in university students and explores whether exercise intensity, intervention period, exercise session duration, participant type and task paradigm are associated with variability in the intervention effects.

Previous research generally supports the notion that aerobic exercise has a certain promotional effect on executive function; however, findings regarding inhibitory control have not been entirely consistent (Chang et al., 2025; Ciria et al., 2018; Kao et al., 2022; Remiszewski et al., 2025). Some studies have found that both single-session and long-term aerobic exercise can improve performance in conflict processing and response inhibition, whilst others have not observed consistent effects (Ciria et al., 2018; Remiszewski et al., 2025). These discrepancies may be related to the use of varying exercise intensities, modes of exercise and inhibitory tasks across previous studies (Aziz-Safaie et al., 2024; Bailey et al., 2021; Youssef et al., 2024). Building upon these studies, the present study further demonstrates, through quantitative meta-analysis that aerobic exercise has an overall small-effect-size improvement on inhibitory control in university students, thereby providing comprehensive evidence to reconcile the inconsistent findings observed in previous individual studies. It should be noted that this effect reflects the overall average results of different aerobic exercise programmes, rather than a fixed effect of any specific exercise programme. Furthermore, single acute exercise sessions and long-term exercise training occur on different time scales, and their effects on inhibitory control may involve different physiological and cognitive processes. Therefore, the overall pooled effect in this study should be interpreted as the average effect across different forms of aerobic exercise exposure, rather than implying that acute exercise and long-term training share the same mechanism of action or pattern of effects. Upon further analysis restricting the inclusion to studies on long-term exercise training alone, the direction and magnitude of the effect were similar to those of the overall analysis, although the confidence interval extended slightly across 0, suggesting that the overall effect was not clearly driven by studies on acute exercise, whilst the precision of the evidence from long-term training remains limited.

The potential mechanisms by which aerobic exercise improves inhibitory control may involve exercise-induced short-term physiological changes and long-term neural adaptations (Youssef et al., 2024). Previous research suggests that aerobic exercise may be associated with changes in physiological arousal, cerebral haemodynamics, neurotrophic factors and prefrontal-related neural activity, thereby providing a potential neurophysiological explanation for the relationship between aerobic exercise and inhibitory control (Bailey et al., 2021; Ludyga et al., 2024). It should be emphasised that the outcomes used for effect size pooling in this meta-analysis were all measures from behavioural tasks such as the Stroop and Flanker tests; no quantitative pooling was performed for neurophysiological indicators such as cerebral blood flow, neurotrophic factors, or EEG, fNIRS and fMRI. Consequently, the mechanisms described above serve merely as theoretical explanations based on previous research, rather than findings directly supported by this meta-analysis; the relevant mechanisms still require further validation in subsequent studies.

Exploratory moderation analyses indicated that exercise intensity, intervention period, exercise session duration, participant type and task paradigm all showed no statistically significant between-group differences. Notably, moderate-intensity exercise showed a numerically larger effect estimate than high-intensity exercise; this is consistent to some extent with findings from some previous studies suggesting that moderate-intensity aerobic exercise may be more beneficial for inhibitory control (Chang et al., 2025). Previous research has suggested that one possible explanation is that moderate-intensity exercise may enhance physiological arousal and cognitive readiness, whilst avoiding the fatigue and competition for resources associated with higher-intensity exercise (Bailey et al., 2021). However, as neither the differences between the intensity subgroups nor the results of the meta-regression reached statistical significance, the current evidence is insufficient to confirm that moderate-intensity exercise is superior to high-intensity exercise, let alone to establish a consistent U-shaped dose–response relationship. Similarly, longer exercise session duration showed a certain advantage in terms of effect size, but the differences between groups were not significant, suggesting that the effects of exercise intensity and duration may be jointly influenced by factors such as exercise mode, total workload and the timing of testing (Chang et al., 2025).

Participant type, intervention period and task paradigm likewise showed no statistically significant between-group differences. Both special populations and general university students exhibited an effect direction favourable to exercise, and the pooled estimates for single-session exercise and long-term interventions were also in the same direction. However, given the limited number of studies within each subgroup, these non-significant differences should not be interpreted as evidence that the effects were equivalent across participant groups or intervention periods, or that these factors do not moderate the intervention effect. The special populations themselves also encompassed diverse characteristics, including overweight status, internet or smartphone addiction and depressive symptoms. The effect sizes obtained from the Flanker and Stroop tasks were numerically similar; however, this should likewise not be interpreted as evidence of equivalent effects across task paradigms, particularly given the differences between these paradigms in stimulus characteristics, conflict processing and response demands (Aziz-Safaie et al., 2024). A further exploratory univariable meta-regression also did not identify any statistically significant moderating associations; given the limited number of independent studies, these findings should be regarded as exploratory and interpreted with caution. Consequently, the current evidence is better suited to describing trends in potential effects than to determining the presence or absence of specific moderating effects or identifying the optimal exercise programme.

Certain limitations should be acknowledged. Firstly, the number of independent studies included was limited, and none were assessed as having an overall low risk of bias; two of the studies were classified as having a high risk of bias, which limits the certainty of the conclusions. Furthermore, all nine included studies were conducted in China; therefore, the current findings primarily reflect a sample of Chinese university students, and caution should be exercised when generalising the results to university student populations with different cultural, educational and geographical backgrounds. Secondly, this study restricted the participants to university students aged 18–25, with the aim of focusing on a relatively consistent developmental stage and reducing the heterogeneity that a wider age range might entail. However, the age composition of university students may vary across different countries and educational systems, and some students may be over 25 years of age; therefore, the applicability of the current findings to older university student populations requires further validation. Thirdly, there are few long-term follow-up studies; the existing evidence mainly reflects the effects of acute or short-term interventions, and the long-term maintenance of the benefits of aerobic exercise on inhibitory control remains unclear. Fourthly, some studies employed multi-arm designs, and differences between studies in terms of exercise intensity, duration and intervention methods have increased the complexity of identifying moderating effects. Furthermore, as pooled analyses and moderating analyses retain information at different levels of detail, direct numerical comparisons of the corresponding estimates are not appropriate. Fifth, some subgroups comprise only a small number of studies, limiting the statistical power of between-group comparisons. Subgroups of specific populations include samples with varying characteristics—such as overweight individuals, those with internet or smartphone addiction, and those with depressive symptoms—resulting in considerable within-group heterogeneity; therefore, the relevant findings should be interpreted with caution. Sixth, exploratory single-factor meta-regression remains limited in terms of statistical power and estimation accuracy due to the limited number of independent studies. Therefore, future research should include more high-quality, large-sample randomised controlled trials; conduct direct comparisons of different intensities and durations whilst standardising exercise load and measures of inhibitory control; and incorporate long-term follow-up and neurophysiological indicators to further clarify the characteristics and potential mechanisms by which aerobic exercise improves inhibitory control in university students.

5

Concllusion

Although the certainty of the existing evidence remains limited, the results of this meta-analysis suggest that aerobic exercise may lead to a modest improvement in university students’ performance on inhibitory control tasks; however, the practical significance of this effect remains unclear, and the representativeness and generalisability of the current evidence are still subject to certain limitations. Exploratory analyses did not reveal any statistically significant moderating associations between the intervention effect and participant type, intervention period, exercise intensity, exercise session duration, or task paradigm, although some subgroups exhibited certain differences in effect sizes. Given the limited number of independent studies, these non-significant findings should not be interpreted as evidence of equivalent effects across subgroups or the absence of moderation. Overall, the available evidence provides preliminary quantitative support for the notion that aerobic exercise may improve inhibitory control in university students; however, these conclusions require further validation through additional high-quality studies to clarify the roles of different exercise parameters and their dose–response relationships.

articles.title: The relationship between family capital and academic burnout among undergraduate sports majors: the mediating role of academic self-efficacy
articles.author: Yang Lan
articles.summary:
Background

Academic burnout is a concern among undergraduate sports majors. Although previous studies have emphasized training- and school-related stressors, less is known about the role of family resources and related psychological mechanisms.

Objective

This study examined the associations among family capital, academic self-efficacy, and academic burnout, including differences across family capital dimensions and the mediating role of academic self-efficacy.

Methods

This cross-sectional study included 325 first- and second-year students enrolled in sports-related degree programs at a sports university in Yunnan Province, China. Pearson correlation, one-way ANOVA, and mediation analysis using PROCESS Model 4 with 5,000 bootstrap resamples were conducted.

Results

Family capital was positively associated with academic self-efficacy (r = 0.554, p < 0.001) and negatively associated with academic burnout (r = −0.575, p < 0.001). Cultural and social capital were significantly associated with higher self-efficacy and lower burnout, whereas economic capital was not significantly associated with burnout. Students with lower family capital reported lower self-efficacy and higher burnout. Academic self-efficacy partially mediated the association between family capital and burnout (B = −0.52, 95% CI [−0.66, −0.40]), accounting for 44.33% of the total effect.

Conclusion

Family capital was associated with academic burnout among undergraduate sports majors, with stronger associations for cultural and social capital than for economic capital. Academic self-efficacy represented a partial mediating pathway. Universities should provide targeted academic guidance, learning support, and educational and career information for students with limited family resources and lower academic self-efficacy.

Introduction

University students’ learning adaptation and psychological development are increasingly recognized as important concerns in higher education research. Academic burnout refers to a negative psychological state characterized by low mood, academic withdrawal, and reduced academic accomplishment in response to sustained academic pressure. It typically manifests as declining learning interest, reduced classroom participation, academic procrastination, self-denial, and helplessness regarding academic outcomes (Maslach et al., 2001; Schaufeli et al., 2002; Lian et al., 2005). A cross-sectional survey of 22,983 Chinese university students reported that approximately 59.9% experienced varying degrees of academic burnout, with nearly 5% reporting severe to extremely severe symptoms (Liu et al., 2023). Latent profile research further indicates substantial heterogeneity in academic burnout among Chinese university students, with low-, moderate-, and high-burnout profiles accounting for 18.15%, 50.88%, and 30.97%, respectively (Li et al., 2026). This issue has important academic consequences. A meta-analysis by Madigan and Curran (2021) showed that student burnout was significantly and negatively associated with academic achievement, and that emotional exhaustion, academic disengagement, and reduced efficacy were all linked to poorer academic performance. Recent studies suggest that academic burnout emerges from the combined influence of academic stress, motivational depletion, reduced learning engagement, and weakened competence beliefs (Ma, 2024; Qin et al., 2025). For example, Wang et al. (2024) found that academic self-efficacy negatively predicted academic burnout among university students, with intrinsic motivation and learning engagement serving as sequential mediators. Cong et al. (2024) also identified learning engagement and academic self-efficacy as important psychological and behavioral factors associated with students’ academic burnout. Thus, students’ vulnerability to burnout depends not only on external academic pressure but also on their competence beliefs, learning engagement, and psychological resources.

Academic burnout among undergraduate sports majors is particularly complex and context-dependent. Their learning activities span classrooms, training fields, and competitive settings, where coursework, specialized training, skill assessment, physical exertion, competition performance, and injury risk jointly shape their daily stressors. Previous studies have shown that student-athletes must continuously balance academic commitments with athletic training demands, which may expose them to time conflicts, physical fatigue, role pressure, and psychological adjustment difficulties (Dorsch et al., 2016; Thompson et al., 2024; De Maio et al., 2025). Exhaustion experienced in the athletic domain may also spill over into the academic domain. Xu et al. (2025) found that athletic burnout among university student-athletes significantly predicted academic burnout, with emotion regulation and sleep quality serving as mediators. However, sports majors exposed to similar academic and training pressures may still differ in their levels of academic burnout. Recent studies have shown that social and psychological resources help explain such differences: parental, teacher, and peer support are associated with behavioral engagement and school burnout among student-athletes; life stress may influence athletic burnout through mindfulness and cognitive emotion regulation; and success expectations and parental emotional support may affect the developmental trajectories of athletic burnout and school burnout (Kuokkanen et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2025; Saarinen et al., 2025).

Family capital provides a useful lens for explaining variation in academic burnout among undergraduate sports majors. Drawing on Bourdieu’s theory of capital, field, and habitus, family economic, cultural, and social capital can be converted within the educational field and shape students’ perceptions of learning, competition, failure, and future development (Bourdieu, 2011; Bourdieu and Passeron, 1990). Conceptually, family capital differs from family functioning and emotional support. Family functioning reflects family relationships and organization (Rhodes et al., 2024), whereas emotional support refers to affective encouragement and understanding (Bueno et al., 2022). Family capital, by contrast, concerns the economic, cultural, and social resources available within the family. Family background may influence students’ learning engagement, academic performance, professional identity, and psychological adjustment through economic security, cultural climate, educational expectations, social networks, and emotional support (Qiu and Ye, 2023; Djekourmane et al., 2025; Li et al., 2024). For undergraduate sports majors, family capital may include economic support, exposure to family sports culture, occupational resources, social networks, and access to information relevant to professional development (Wheeler, 2012; Dorsch et al., 2016). Failure in sports-related learning is often public and embodied; unsuccessful skill demonstrations, poor physical fitness test results, and competition losses may make competence differences highly visible. Family capital may therefore influence how students make sense of such failure experiences. Existing studies indicate that parenting styles may shape students’ learning behaviors through causal attribution and self-efficacy; students who attribute failure to low ability are more likely to experience helplessness, whereas positive family functioning and supportive parent–child relationships may reduce academic burnout by enhancing academic self-efficacy (Li et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2025). The capital perspective therefore complements research on family functioning and emotional support by shifting attention from relational quality and affective exchanges to the economic, cultural, and social resources that families possess and can mobilize to support students’ educational adaptation.

Based on these considerations, this study aimed to examine the associations among family capital, academic self-efficacy, and academic burnout among undergraduate sports majors. Specifically, we examined whether the associations with academic burnout differed across the economic, cultural, and social dimensions of family capital and whether academic self-efficacy mediated the association between overall family capital and academic burnout. Accordingly, the following hypothesis was proposed:

H1: Family capital is negatively associated with academic burnout among undergraduate sports majors.

Academic self-efficacy may serve as a key psychological mechanism linking family capital to academic burnout. It refers to students’ judgments of their capacity to complete coursework, master professional skills, regulate learning strategies, and cope with academic setbacks (Artino, 2012; Zajacova et al., 2005). Self-efficacy theory suggests that individuals’ beliefs about their abilities influence their effort, persistence, and behavioral choices when they encounter difficulties (Bandura, 1997). Higher academic self-efficacy may help students cope with challenges and sustain learning engagement, whereas lower academic self-efficacy may weaken learning motivation and increase procrastination, avoidance, emotional exhaustion, and reduced accomplishment (Wang et al., 2024; Rad et al., 2025). Previous studies on family-related factors have shown that family functioning, family cultural capital, social support, and parental involvement are associated with higher academic self-efficacy, and that stronger academic self-efficacy is linked to lower academic burnout, greater learning motivation, stronger learning engagement, and better academic adjustment (Brouwer et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025; Zhu, 2025). For example, Yang et al. (2025) found that academic self-efficacy mediated the relationship between family functioning and academic burnout. Although family functioning is conceptually distinct from family capital, this evidence suggests that family-related conditions may be associated with academic burnout partly through self-efficacy. For undergraduate sports majors, greater family capital may provide access to problem-solving resources and a clearer sense of certainty about future development. This sense of certainty may strengthen students’ perceived control over academic tasks and training difficulties, thereby enhancing their academic self-efficacy. Among sports majors, competence beliefs may be shaped by course grades, training performance, skill assessments, physical fitness levels, and competition results. Academic self-efficacy may therefore be central to explaining variation in academic burnout within this group. Accordingly, this study proposes the following hypotheses:

H2: Family capital positively predicts academic self-efficacy among undergraduate sports majors. H3: Academic self-efficacy negatively predicts academic burnout among undergraduate sports majors.

The influence of family capital on academic burnout may operate through students’ psychological processes. Economic capital may support learning, training, and competition by providing access to training equipment, competition expenses, and extracurricular training resources. Cultural capital may shape students’ understanding of professional value, frustration, and developmental pathways through the family educational climate, parents’ educational experiences, and exposure to sports culture. Social capital may help students obtain information about further education, employment, and career development through relatives’ occupational resources, social networks, and industry information channels (Wheeler, 2012; Sheridan et al., 2014; Djekourmane et al., 2025). Whether these resources reduce academic burnout may depend on their transformation into competence beliefs when students face academic and training difficulties. Students with higher academic self-efficacy are more likely to interpret course pressure, training setbacks, and skill failures as manageable challenges. By contrast, students with limited family capital and weaker academic self-efficacy may be more vulnerable to low mood, academic withdrawal, and reduced accomplishment (Wang et al., 2024; Rad et al., 2025). Existing studies have examined the associations among family resources, academic self-efficacy, and academic burnout (Wang et al., 2024; Öztürk Çelik, 2025; Yang et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2025). However, the pathway through which family capital influences academic burnout via academic self-efficacy among undergraduate sports majors remains insufficiently understood. Therefore, this study proposes the following hypothesis:

H4: Academic self-efficacy mediates the relationship between family capital and academic burnout among undergraduate sports majors.

Existing research has mainly examined burnout among sports majors from the perspectives of training stress, athletic burnout, and school support, but has paid less attention to how family resources shape students’ psychological processes related to learning. By integrating family capital, academic self-efficacy, and academic burnout into a unified model, the present study extends this literature from a predominantly training- and school-related perspective to a family-resource perspective. The findings may provide evidence to help universities identify students with limited family capital, strengthen their academic self-efficacy, and reduce their risk of academic burnout.

Methods

Research design

This study used a cross-sectional survey design. An anonymous online questionnaire was used to examine the association between family capital and academic burnout among undergraduate sports majors in China and to test whether academic self-efficacy mediated this association. The questionnaire collected demographic information, family capital indicators, and scale-based measures of academic self-efficacy and academic burnout. The study was reported in accordance with the STROBE guidelines (von Elm et al., 2007).

Participants

Participants were first- and second-year undergraduate students majoring in sports-related disciplines at a sports university in Yunnan Province, China. First- and second-year students were selected to reduce heterogeneity associated with upper-year internships, career preparation, and graduation-related academic demands, which may independently affect academic burnout. A stratified cluster random sampling procedure was used. Students were first stratified by grade and sport specialization. Within each stratum, eligible classes were assigned identification numbers, and classes were randomly selected using a computer-generated random-number procedure. All eligible students in the selected classes were invited to participate. The number of classes selected from each stratum was approximately proportional to the size of the corresponding student population.

The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) being a full-time first- or second-year undergraduate student enrolled in a sports-related major at the university; (2) providing informed consent and participating voluntarily; and (3) being able to complete the questionnaire independently. The exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) incomplete questionnaires; (2) an unusually short completion time; (3) patterned or invariant responses; and (4) missing key information or logical inconsistencies. A total of 377 questionnaires were distributed, of which 347 were returned. After 22 invalid questionnaires were excluded, 325 valid responses were retained, yielding an effective response rate of 93.66%. Instruments

Demographic and sport-related characteristics

Demographic and sport-related information was collected using five self-report items: sex, grade, age, sport specialization, and years of sports training. The distribution of these characteristics is presented in Table 1.

Family capital

Family capital was conceptualized as a multidimensional construct comprising economic, cultural, and social capital. Drawing on Bourdieu’s theory of capital and the operational framework of Su et al. (2025), and considering the characteristics of undergraduate sports majors, the family capital measure consisted of nine items across three dimensions.

Economic capital comprised two items: monthly family income and the family’s capacity to afford educational expenses. Monthly family income was coded into five ascending categories: 1 = <5,000 RMB, 2 = 5,000–9,999 RMB, 3 = 10,000–14,999 RMB, 4 = 15,000–19,999 RMB, and 5 = ≥20,000 RMB. The family’s capacity to afford educational expenses was assessed on a five-point scale: 1 = completely unable to afford, 2 = difficult to afford, 3 = basically able to afford, 4 = relatively easy to afford, and 5 = fully able to afford. The two item scores were summed to obtain the economic capital score, with a theoretical range of 2–10. Higher scores indicated greater family economic capital.

Cultural capital comprised four items: paternal educational attainment, maternal educational attainment, family attention to sports events and sports culture, and family sports atmosphere. Paternal and maternal educational attainment were each coded into five categories: 1 = junior high school education or below, 2 = senior high school education, 3 = junior college education, 4 = bachelor’s degree, and 5 = master’s degree or above. Family attention to sports events and sports culture and family sports atmosphere were each rated on a five-point scale ranging from 1 = very low to 5 = very high. The four item scores were summed to obtain the cultural capital score, with a theoretical range of 4–20. Higher scores indicated greater family cultural capital.

Social capital comprised three items: paternal occupational status, maternal occupational status, and the occupational status of close relatives. Based on China’s occupational structure and the International Standard Classification of Occupations (ISCO) (International Labour Office, 2012), each item was coded into five categories: 1 = unskilled workers, agricultural laborers, and other low-skilled occupations; 2 = service workers, general clerical workers, and ordinary operational positions; 3 = skilled workers, technical employees, and front-line management positions; 4 = professionals and middle-level managers; and 5 = senior managers, senior professionals, and other occupations associated with greater social resources. The three item scores were summed to obtain the social capital score, with a theoretical range of 3–15. Higher scores indicated greater family social capital.

The nine item scores were summed to obtain the overall family capital score, yielding a theoretical range of 9–45, with higher scores indicating greater family capital. In the present sample, the observed ranges were 2–10 for economic capital, 4–18 for cultural capital, and 3–15 for social capital. In this study, Cronbach’s α for the overall family capital measure was 0.845. Cronbach’s α values for the economic, cultural, and social capital dimensions were 0.880, 0.866, and 0.832, respectively. The KMO value was 0.816, and Bartlett’s test of sphericity was significant (p < 0.001).

Academic self-efficacy

This study used the Academic Self-Efficacy Scale developed by Liang (2004) to assess academic self-efficacy among undergraduate sports majors. The scale consists of 22 items across two dimensions: academic ability self-efficacy and academic behavior self-efficacy, with 11 items in each dimension. Academic ability self-efficacy reflects individuals’ judgments of their capacity to complete learning tasks and meet academic requirements. Academic behavior self-efficacy reflects individuals’ confidence in initiating, sustaining, and regulating learning behaviors. All items were rated on a five-point Likert scale ranging from 1 = completely disagree to 5 = completely agree. Higher scores indicated greater academic self-efficacy. In this study, Cronbach’s α for the overall scale was 0.873. Cronbach’s α values for the academic ability and academic behavior self-efficacy dimensions were 0.757 and 0.753, respectively. The KMO value was 0.894, and Bartlett’s test of sphericity was significant (p < 0.001).

Academic burnout

This study used the College Student Academic Burnout Scale, translated and revised by Lian et al. (2005), to assess academic burnout among undergraduate sports majors. Based on Maslach’s theory of burnout, the scale consists of 20 items across three dimensions: low mood, inappropriate behavior, and low academic achievement (reflecting reduced personal accomplishment rather than objective academic performance). Conceptually, this dimension differs from academic self-efficacy, which concerns students’ beliefs about their capability to perform academic tasks and regulate learning behaviors. Items 1, 3, 6, 8, 11, 13, 15, and 18 were reverse-scored. All items were rated on a five-point Likert scale, with higher total scores indicating greater academic burnout. Following previous applications of the scale (Zhu et al., 2023), participants were classified as having no academic burnout (≤ 40), an uncertain burnout status (41–59), or academic burnout (≥ 60). These categories were used for descriptive purposes only. In this study, Cronbach’s α for the overall scale was 0.920. Cronbach’s α values for the low mood, inappropriate behavior, and low academic achievement dimensions were 0.787, 0.735, and 0.739, respectively. The KMO value was 0.855, and Bartlett’s test of sphericity was significant (p < 0.001).

Procedure

This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of K University (approval number: KM2025125J) and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Data were collected in March 2026. After students were stratified by grade and sport specialization and eligible classes were randomly selected using the computer-generated procedure described above, course instructors in the selected classes distributed the Wenjuanxing questionnaire link to their class groups. Before completing the questionnaire, all participants read an electronic informed consent statement. Participants proceeded to the formal questionnaire only after being informed of the study purpose, anonymity, and the voluntary nature of participation.

The questionnaire was presented in the following order: informed consent, demographic information, family capital measures, academic self-efficacy scale, and academic burnout scale. All items were mandatory, and completion took approximately 20–30 min. The survey was conducted anonymously. Participants received no material compensation, and each IP address was permitted to submit only one response.

After data collection, responses were screened according to prespecified data quality criteria. Responses were excluded if they were incomplete, had an unusually short completion time (< 300 s), showed patterned or invariant responses, or contained logical inconsistencies or missing key information. All data were used solely for academic research purposes. Participants could withdraw at any time during the survey without adverse consequences.

Data analysis

Data were analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics 26.0. First, invalid responses were excluded, and reverse-scored items were recoded. Descriptive statistics, Cronbach’s α coefficients, KMO values, and Bartlett’s tests of sphericity were used to examine sample characteristics and the reliability and validity of the measures. The sample was then divided into low, medium, and high family capital groups based on tertiles of the total family capital score. Pearson correlation analysis was used to examine associations among the main variables, and one-way analysis of variance was used to test group differences. When significant group differences were identified, Tukey’s HSD test was used for post hoc comparisons when the homogeneity of variance assumption was satisfied, whereas the Games–Howell test was used when this assumption was violated. Welch’s robust test was additionally reported when homogeneity of variance was not satisfied. Finally, Model 4 of the PROCESS macro was used to test the mediating role of academic self-efficacy, with 5,000 bootstrap resamples used to estimate 95% confidence intervals. The mediating effect was considered significant when the 95% confidence interval did not include zero. All tests were two-tailed, and statistical significance was set at p < 0.05.

Between-group difference analysis

To compare academic self-efficacy and academic burnout across family capital groups, normality was first assessed for the low, moderate, and high family capital groups. The Shapiro–Wilk test indicated that academic self-efficacy did not significantly deviate from normality across the three groups, with p = 0.923, 0.430, and 0.519, respectively. For academic burnout, the moderate and high family capital groups did not significantly deviate from normality (p = 0.054 and 0.182, respectively), whereas the low family capital group showed a slight deviation from normality (p = 0.035). Given the relatively large group sizes, one-way analysis of variance was conducted, with Welch’s robust test additionally reported where the homogeneity of variance assumption was not met.

Regression and mediation effects

To further examine the mechanism linking family capital to academic burnout, this study specified academic self-efficacy as the mediating variable and tested the mediation model using Model 4 of the SPSS PROCESS macro. Bootstrapping with 5,000 resamples was used to estimate 95% confidence intervals (see Figure 2).

Regression analysis showed that family capital had a significant total effect on academic burnout (B = −1.17, t = −12.624, p < 0.001, 95% CI [−1.35, −0.99]). Family capital positively predicted academic self-efficacy (B = 1.05, t = 11.972, p < 0.001), and academic self-efficacy negatively predicted academic burnout (B = −0.49, t = −9.489, p < 0.001). After academic self-efficacy was included in the model, the direct effect of family capital on academic burnout remained significant (B = −0.65, t = −6.606, p < 0.001, 95% CI [−0.84, −0.46]), indicating partial mediation.

Bootstrap mediation analysis showed that the indirect effect through academic self-efficacy was −0.52. The direct and indirect effects accounted for 55.67 and 44.33% of the total effect, respectively. The 95% bootstrap confidence interval for the indirect effect did not include zero (95% CI [−0.66, −0.40]), indicating that the mediation effect was statistically significant (see Table 5).

Discussion

This study found that family capital was significantly associated with lower academic burnout among undergraduate sports majors. Although participants in the present study were enrolled in sports-related degree programs, research on student-athletes provides a relevant comparison for understanding the academic and sport-related demands encountered in such educational contexts. Previous research has shown that student-athletes are chronically exposed to the dual demands of academic study and athletic training, with training load, academic pressure, competitive performance, and physical fatigue jointly increasing burnout risk (Gould and Whitley, 2009). Xu et al. (2025) further found that athletic burnout among university student-athletes predicted academic burnout, suggesting that exhaustion in the training domain may spill over into the academic domain. Extending this line of research, the present study found that higher family capital was associated with lower academic burnout among undergraduate sports majors. This association suggests that family resources may be relevant to students’ academic adaptation, although the present study did not directly assess training–academic pressure or test whether family capital buffers its effects. In a longitudinal study of student-athletes, Saarinen et al. (2025) found that parental emotional support and success expectations shaped the developmental trajectories of athletic burnout and school burnout. Dorsch et al. (2016) also found that positive parental involvement in student-athletes’ academic and athletic lives was associated with stronger academic self-efficacy and developmental adaptation. Together, these findings extend previous burnout research by highlighting family resources as an additional contextual factor associated with academic adaptation among undergraduate sports majors.

It is notable that economic capital was not significantly associated with academic burnout. This finding is not fully consistent with studies suggesting that insufficient resources increase students’ risk of burnout. One possible explanation is that material resources alone may be less directly related to students’ academic burnout than other forms of family resources. Pennington and Castor (2022) noted that burnout among student-athletes is often associated with competitive pressure, highly professionalized training environments, and excessive time demands. Parental pressure, coaching style, academic burden, and time-management difficulties have also been identified as important sources of burnout among student-athletes (Dubuc-Charbonneau and Durand-Bush, 2018; Thompson et al., 2024). The present findings therefore complement international research focused mainly on training, time pressure, coaching, and self-regulation by highlighting the relevance of family resources to burnout among undergraduate sports majors. This dimension-specific result further suggests that economic capital did not display the same pattern as cultural and social capital. The mechanisms underlying this difference require further investigation.

Compared with economic capital, family cultural capital and social capital were more strongly associated with academic burnout. Cultural capital may provide students with educational expectations, interpretive frameworks, and familiarity with academic and professional development, whereas social capital may facilitate access to information, guidance, social networks, and career-related resources. Families with higher social capital may also provide informational resources related to further education, employment, competition, and career development, thereby reducing students’ sense of helplessness when facing future uncertainty. A sense of belonging has been associated with burnout and graduation expectations among student-athletes, highlighting the importance of supportive relationships for student-athlete adaptation (Fearon et al., 2011). These findings suggest that academic burnout was more strongly associated with cultural and social resources than with material resources alone, highlighting the importance of distinguishing among different forms of family capital rather than treating family capital as a homogeneous construct.

The between-group analysis further supports this interpretation. Students in the low family capital group reported higher levels of academic burnout than those in the moderate and high family capital groups, and these differences were reflected across all three dimensions: low mood, inappropriate behavior, and perceived low academic achievement. This finding extends the correlational results by showing that differences in family capital were reflected not only in overall burnout but also in its emotional, behavioral, and self-evaluative components. Moreover, the graded differences across the low, moderate, and high family capital groups suggest that variation in family resources was systematically associated with students’ academic adjustment rather than being relevant only to an extreme-risk subgroup. Saarinen et al. (2025) found that lower success expectations were associated with higher levels of athletic and school burnout. Together, these findings indicate that differences in family resources may be reflected across multiple aspects of students’ burnout experiences.

This study also found that academic self-efficacy partially mediated the association between family capital and academic burnout. In other words, family capital may be linked to lower burnout by strengthening students’ beliefs in their learning ability and problem-solving capacity. This finding goes beyond the direct association between family capital and burnout by identifying academic self-efficacy as one psychological pathway through which family resources may be related to students’ academic adaptation. Greater family resources may provide access to guidance, information, and problem-solving support that strengthen students’ confidence in managing academic demands. This finding is consistent with Dorsch et al. (2016), who found that parental involvement was associated with stronger academic self-efficacy among student-athletes. In addition, Öztürk Çelik (2025) found that self-efficacy was closely associated with burnout and mental health among student-athletes. Stronger academic self-efficacy may in turn support persistence and more adaptive responses to academic difficulties, thereby reducing vulnerability to burnout.

However, academic self-efficacy only partially mediated this association, suggesting that family capital may be linked to academic burnout through multiple pathways. Beyond academic self-efficacy, resource-related factors such as access to career information, as well as broader family and educational processes such as parental emotional support, professional identity formation, coach–student relationships, and peer support, may also be relevant. These factors were not directly assessed in the present study and should be examined in future research. The partial mediation therefore indicates that academic self-efficacy explains only part of the association between family capital and academic burnout and that a broader framework incorporating family resources, psychological beliefs, and contextual factors may be needed to more fully understand burnout among undergraduate sports majors.

This study contributes to the literature by extending research on academic burnout among undergraduate sports majors from a predominantly training- and school-related perspective to a family resource perspective. By distinguishing the economic, cultural, and social dimensions of family capital and identifying academic self-efficacy as a partial mediator, the study further shows that different forms of family resources may be associated with academic adaptation through both resource-based and psychological pathways. In practice, university physical education departments should pay particular attention to students with limited cultural and social resources and lower academic self-efficacy. Academic guidance, self-efficacy–enhancing learning support, access to educational and career information, and opportunities to strengthen students’ social and informational resources may help support their academic adaptation (Wang et al., 2025).

This study has several limitations. First, the cross-sectional survey design can identify associations among variables but cannot establish causal relationships. Future research should use longitudinal designs to examine the dynamic relationships among family capital, academic self-efficacy, and academic burnout. Second, the sample was drawn from a single sports university, which limits the generalizability of the findings to students from other regions, institutional levels, and sports specializations. Future studies should include larger and more diverse samples across multiple institutions and regions. Third, family capital was assessed based on students’ self-reports, and students may not have complete or fully accurate knowledge of household income or the occupational circumstances of their parents and close relatives. In addition, family capital, academic self-efficacy, and academic burnout were all reported by the same respondent, which may introduce shared-source bias. Future research could incorporate parent-reported family information, objective or administrative indicators, and multi-informant data to improve measurement accuracy. Finally, this study did not fully incorporate sport-specific contextual variables, such as training load, injury history, competition level, coach support, peer relationships, and professional identity. Future research could combine interviews, training performance data, and course grades to clarify how family capital is related to learning confidence and psychological adaptability among sports majors.

Conclusion

This study addressed its objectives by examining the associations among family capital, academic self-efficacy, and academic burnout among undergraduate sports majors, comparing the associations across different dimensions of family capital, and testing the mediating role of academic self-efficacy. Overall family capital was negatively associated with academic burnout and positively associated with academic self-efficacy, while academic self-efficacy was negatively associated with academic burnout. Accordingly, H1, H2, and H3 were supported. Academic self-efficacy also partially mediated the association between overall family capital and academic burnout, providing support for H4. The dimension-specific analyses further showed that cultural and social capital were significantly associated with lower academic burnout and higher academic self-efficacy, whereas economic capital was only weakly associated with academic self-efficacy and was not significantly associated with academic burnout. These findings indicate that different forms of family capital are not equally associated with academic adaptation and directly address the study objective of examining differences across family capital dimensions. Taken together, the findings suggest that family capital, particularly cultural and social resources, is associated with academic burnout among undergraduate sports majors, with academic self-efficacy representing a partial mediating pathway. Universities should therefore pay particular attention to students with limited cultural and social resources and lower academic self-efficacy and provide targeted academic guidance, learning support, and access to educational and career-related information.

articles.title: Associations between bullying, depressive symptoms, parental supervision, and suicidal behaviors in Chinese adolescents: a cross-sectional study
articles.author: La Mang
articles.summary: BackgroundSchool bullying is associated with elevated risk of adolescent mental health problems, yet the complex interrelationships between bullying experiences, depressive symptoms, and parental factors in the Chinese cultural context require further investigation. This cross-sectional study examined associations between traditional and cyberbullying (as victim or perpetrator), depressive symptoms, parental supervision, and suicidal behaviors among Chinese adolescents.MethodsData from 12,019 students (Grades 5–12) recruited from 16 administrative districts in Beijing through a cross-sectional survey using multi-stage cluster random sampling were included in the final analyses. Participants completed standardized measures of traditional and cyberbullying (victimization and perpetration), depressive symptoms, suicidal behaviors, and parental supervision. Associations among variables were examined using chi-square tests, ANOVA, and correlation analyses. Indirect and conditional associations were examined using PROCESS Models 4 and 59, respectively, with 5,000 percentile bootstrap resamples, adjusting for demographic and psychosocial covariates.ResultsAmong 12,019 participants, 1,322 (11.0%) reported suicidal behaviors. All forms of bullying were significantly associated with both depressive symptoms and suicidal behaviors. Depressive symptoms were associated with both bullying experiences and suicidality, consistent with a potential mediating pathway. The associations between bullying involvement and depressive symptoms, as well as between depressive symptoms and suicidal behaviors, were stronger at higher levels of perceived parental supervision.ConclusionThis cross-sectional study documented significant associations between bullying, depressive symptoms, parental supervision, and suicidal behaviors among Chinese adolescents. While depressive symptoms may represent a key psychological pathway linking bullying to suicidality, the conditional associations observed suggest that parental supervision may interact with these processes in complex ways. Longitudinal research is needed to clarify causal pathways and inform culturally sensitive prevention strategies.

articles.title: Academic motivation and basic psychological needs among university students in physical education and mountain sports: a self-determination theory study
articles.author: Stefan Alecu
articles.summary: Academic motivation in physically demanding university programmes may be better understood by considering motivational quality rather than motivation quantity alone. This cross-sectional observational survey supplemented by structured content analysis examined relationships among basic psychological need satisfaction and frustration, autonomous motivation, controlled motivation, amotivation, continuation intention, and career commitment in first- and second-year students enrolled in Physical Education and Mountain Sports at Transilvania University of Brașov. Data were collected from 6 to 30 October 2025 after ethics approval, yielding a final analytical sample of 237 students. Participants completed the Academic Motivation Scale-College/University version, the Basic Psychological Need Satisfaction and Frustration Scale, contextual and sport-related items, continuation and career indicators, and two open-ended prompts. Original open-ended answers were standardized into 50 motivation and 50 demotivation formulations and independently coded by both authors. Autonomous motivation averaged 5.04 (SD = 1.05), amotivation 2.40 (SD = 0.95), overall need satisfaction 3.72 (SD = 0.73), and overall need frustration 2.21 (SD = 0.76). Need satisfaction correlated strongly with autonomous motivation (Spearman ρ = 0.704), whereas need frustration correlated strongly with amotivation (ρ = 0.661). In adjusted models, need satisfaction was positively associated with autonomous motivation (β = 0.539, p < 0.001), and need frustration was positively associated with amotivation (β = 0.569, p < 0.001). Human coding agreement was high for motivation (92.0%, κ = 0.898) and demotivation (94.0%, κ = 0.927). Teaching/prosocial impact was the most frequent motivation category (33.8%), while curriculum/teaching/assessment was the most frequent demotivation category (23.6%). Overall, self-reported need satisfaction and frustration were differentially associated with motivational quality in this cohort, but the cross-sectional, single-faculty design precludes causal or population-level conclusions.

articles.title: Psychological pathways linking body mass index and depression in women and men in a Colombian sociodemographic context
articles.author: Duban Romero
articles.summary: Body mass index (BMI) shows inconsistent associations with depressive symptoms, and it remains unclear whether body self-esteem and eating disorder symptoms mediate this association, and whether this mediation differs by gender. Therefore, this study used multigroup structural equation modeling to examine these mediators in Colombian young adults, separately for women and men. A total of 662 participants aged 18 to 30 years (398 women, 60.1%; Mage = 21.75, SD = 3.11) were recruited through snowball sampling and completed an online survey with self-reported weight and height and validated measures of body self-esteem, eating disorder symptoms and depressive symptoms. BMI showed no total association with depressive symptoms in women or men. Nevertheless, higher BMI was associated with lower body self-esteem and more eating disorder symptoms, and both mediators were associated with more depressive symptoms, yielding positive indirect effects in women (b = 0.033, 95% CI [0.022, 0.045]) and men (b = 0.015, 95% CI [0.006, 0.028]). In men, mediation was indirect-only, whereas in women a negative direct effect offset the indirect effect, a pattern of competitive mediation. The path from BMI to eating disorder symptoms was stronger in women, but the relative weight of the two pathways did not differ by gender. Body self-esteem and eating disorder symptoms link BMI to depressive symptoms in both women and men, with quantitative rather than qualitative gender differences, which suggests that both processes deserve attention in prevention and intervention efforts with young adults.

articles.title: Effects of self-regulated learning prompts on statistical problem-solving by goal orientation
articles.author: Aeng Muhidin
articles.summary: Complex statistical problem-solving requires students to plan, monitor, and evaluate their own thinking, yet instructional interventions designed to support this self-regulation often produce inconsistent results. This study examined whether a metacognitive-prompt intervention grounded in self-regulated learning (SRL) theory was associated with university students’ statistical problem-solving ability, and whether this association depended on students’ achievement goal orientation (mastery vs. performance). A quasi-experimental, nonequivalent control-group pretest-posttest design with a 2 × 2 factorial structure (class × orientation) was used with 21 students from two intact classes (experimental n = 10, control n = 11); because class was assigned at the classroom rather than the individual level, the study is best characterized as a small, single-site pilot comparison. Achievement goal orientation was measured with an instrument adapted from a 2 × 2 achievement goal framework, and statistical problem-solving was measured with a 10-item complex multiple-choice test. Two-way ANOVA on normalized gain (N-gain) scores, supported by ANCOVA controlling for pretest, showed no statistically significant main effect of the metacognitive-prompt intervention, F (1,17) = 0.02, p = 0.882, partial η2 = 0.001, 95% CI [0.00, 0.46]; no significant main effect of achievement goal orientation, F (1,17) = 1.59, p = 0.224, partial η2 = 0.086, 95% CI [0.00, 0.54]; and no significant interaction between the two, F (1,17) = 0.08, p = 0.779, partial η2 = 0.005, 95% CI [0.00, 0.47]. A sensitivity analysis showed the design had 80% power to detect only very large effects (partial η2 ≥ 0.30), and equivalence tests did not support concluding that the true effects were negligible. All four groups achieved a moderate mean N-gain (0.30–0.70). These findings do not support the hypothesized aptitude-treatment interaction; rather than showing that prompting has no effect, this exploratory, underpowered comparison detected no statistically significant differential benefit across goal orientations, and a larger, multi-classroom design is needed for a confirmatory test.

articles.title: Age-specific associations between perceptions of community environmental quality, restorative environmental perception and community identity: an interpretative perspective based on the Homo Urbanicus
articles.author: Chenda Guo
articles.summary: ContextUnderstanding the associations between residents’ perceived community environmental quality and community identity, and their age-related differences, is important for advancing all-age-friendly communities.MethodsDrawing on Hok-Lin Leung’s Homo Urbanicus theory, this study analyzed 929 questionnaires collected in 2025 from 36 residential communities in Yangpu District, Shanghai. Structural equation modelling was used to examine the association structure among perceived community environmental quality, perceived restorative environment and community identity, and to test whether the three structural paths differ across four age groups (children, young adults, middle-aged and older adults), using measurement invariance tests, cross-group equality constraints and paired parameter comparisons, with cluster-robust standard errors.Results(1) Perceived restorative environment significantly mediated the association between perceived community environmental quality and community identity: the indirect effect accounted for 51.5% of the total effect and the direct effect remained significant, the two links being comparable in magnitude. (2) Measurement invariance was broadly supported, permitting cross-group comparison of the structural paths, and the mediation held in all four groups (bias-corrected bootstrap, 5,000 resamples). Cross-group differences were localized: the path from perceived restorative environment to community identity was stronger in the middle-aged than in the older group (cluster-robust difference = 0.270, p = 0.021; significant under all three specifications). The children’s group scored numerically higher on the path from perceived community environmental quality to perceived restorative environment, but this did not consistently reach significance and is reported descriptively. Direct effects did not differ significantly across the four groups (Δχ2 = 2.670, Δdf = 3, p = 0.445), so the non-significant direct effect in the children’s group is not interpreted as an absent effect.DiscussionThese findings are associations derived from cross-sectional data, not causal effects or observed psychological transformation. Within the ‘events, people, time and space’ framework of the Homo Urbanicus theory, life-stage differences in the weighting of self-existence and coexistence needs offer a coherent interpretation of the age-specific path patterns. The results support the differentiated provision of restorative space in age-friendly community planning.

articles.title: Adolescent ICT use profiles and creative thinking: evidence from 42 countries in PISA 2022
articles.author: Can Meşe
articles.summary: Research on information and communication technology (ICT) use and educational outcomes has reported positive, negative, and null associations, and little is known about creative thinking, which Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) assessed for the first time in 2022. This study examined how profiles of ICT use relate to creative thinking and whether profile membership predicts creative thinking beyond the dimensions of use from which the profiles are derived. Using data from a large international sample of PISA 2022 students, latent profile analysis of the six Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) dimensions of ICT use identified four profiles that differed mainly in the overall level of use. Creative thinking was compared across profiles using all plausible values, replicate weights and a bias-adjusted three-step approach, and random forest models compared the predictive value of the profiles and the dimensions. Students with below-average use scored highest, followed by those with above-average use, whereas students with very low and very high use scored lowest. The low scores at the two ends had different correlates: adjustment for socioeconomic status and gender substantially reduced the gap for very low use but left the gap for very high use almost unchanged. In the random forest models, the six dimensions predicted creative thinking better than profile membership did. Partial dependence plots showed higher predicted scores with more school activities outside the classroom and lower predicted scores with high weekday leisure use and more support or feedback via ICT. The findings suggest that the association between ICT use and creative thinking is not linear, and that profiles based on the level of use are useful for describing groups of students but carry less information than the dimensions of use.
